abstract: We consider different types of single-hidden-Iayer feedforward nets: with or without direct input to output connections, and using either thresh(cid:173) old or sigmoidal activation functions. The main results show that direct connections in threshold nets double the recognition but not the interpo(cid:173) lation power, while using sigmoids rather than thresholds allows (at least) doubling both. Various results are also given on VC dimension and other measures of recognition capabilities.
originalAbstract: We consider different types of single-hidden-Iayer feedforward nets: with or without direct input to output connections, and using either thresh(cid:173) old or sigmoidal activation functions. The main results show that direct connections in threshold nets double the recognition but not the interpo(cid:173) lation power, while using sigmoids rather than thresholds allows (at least) doubling both. Various results are also given on VC dimension and other measures of recognition capabilities.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes the capabilities of feedforward neural networks with one hidden layer. It compares two architectural choices: whether inputs connect directly to outputs, and whether units use threshold or sigmoidal activation functions. The focus is on how these choices change what a network can represent.

The results distinguish recognition power from interpolation power. Recognition concerns distinguishing patterns, while interpolation concerns matching specified values at given inputs. For threshold networks, adding direct input-to-output connections doubles recognition power but does not double interpolation power. The same structural addition therefore has different consequences for these two capabilities.

Replacing threshold activations with sigmoids allows at least a doubling of both recognition and interpolation power. The paper also gives results involving VC dimension and other recognition-capacity measures. Together, these findings show why architectural capacity needs more than one description: a change that expands one kind of representational ability need not expand another in the same way. The activation function and the availability of direct connections play distinct roles in these comparisons.
summary.tldr: Direct connections and sigmoid activations increase single-hidden-layer network capacity in different ways for recognition and interpolation.

title: Remarks on Interpolation and Recognition Using Neural Nets

abstract: Barto, Sutton and Watkins [2] introduced a grid task as a didactic ex(cid:173) ample of temporal difference planning and asynchronous dynamical pre>(cid:173) gramming. This paper considers the effects of changing the coding of the input stimulus, and demonstrates that the self-supervised learning of a particular form of hidden unit representation improves performance.
originalAbstract: Barto, Sutton and Watkins [2] introduced a grid task as a didactic ex(cid:173) ample of temporal difference planning and asynchronous dynamical pre>(cid:173) gramming. This paper considers the effects of changing the coding of the input stimulus, and demonstrates that the self-supervised learning of a particular form of hidden unit representation improves performance.

paragraphs: This paper revisits a grid task used to illustrate temporal-difference planning and asynchronous dynamic programming. Its focus is the representation of the input stimulus: how information about the task is encoded before the learning and planning process uses it. The study asks how changing that encoding affects performance on the navigation problem.

The authors examine a particular hidden-unit representation learned through self-supervision. This introduces a learned intermediate representation between the supplied stimulus and the system's task processing. The representation itself becomes something that the system acquires, making input coding part of the learning problem rather than only a fixed design choice.

The reported finding is that learning this hidden representation improves performance. That result gives representation learning a concrete role within the grid-task setting: the information available to the planner becomes more useful through the way it is encoded. The paper's contribution is to show that the performance of this temporal-difference planning task depends on the learned internal representation as well as the planning procedure.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised learning of a hidden representation improves performance on a grid task for temporal-difference planning.

title: Navigating through Temporal Difference

abstract: In this paper we propose an extension to the RAAM by Pollack. This extension, the Labeling RAAM (LRAAM), can encode la(cid:173) beled graphs with cycles by representing pointers explicitly. Data encoded in an LRAAM can be accessed by pointer as well as by content. Direct access by content can be achieved by transform(cid:173) ing the encoder network of the LRAAM into an analog Hopfield network with hidden units. Different access procedures can be defined depending on the access key. Sufficient conditions on the asymptotical stability of the associated Hopfield network are briefly introduced.
originalAbstract: In this paper we propose an extension to the RAAM by Pollack. This extension, the Labeling RAAM (LRAAM), can encode la(cid:173) beled graphs with cycles by representing pointers explicitly. Data encoded in an LRAAM can be accessed by pointer as well as by content. Direct access by content can be achieved by transform(cid:173) ing the encoder network of the LRAAM into an analog Hopfield network with hidden units. Different access procedures can be defined depending on the access key. Sufficient conditions on the asymptotical stability of the associated Hopfield network are briefly introduced.

paragraphs: This paper extends RAAM with a representation called Labeling RAAM, or LRAAM, for encoding labeled graphs that can contain cycles. Its central mechanism is to represent pointers explicitly. These pointers make references between graph elements part of the encoding, including relationships that loop back to previously connected elements.

The resulting representation supports two forms of access. Data can be retrieved through a pointer, following an explicit reference, or through its content. To achieve direct content-based access, the authors transform the LRAAM encoder into an analog Hopfield network with hidden units. They also describe the possibility of different access procedures depending on the key supplied for retrieval.

This combination matters because graph connectivity and information retrieval become parts of the same neural representation. The method addresses both how a cyclic structure is stored and how its contents can subsequently be reached. The paper also briefly introduces sufficient conditions for asymptotic stability of the associated Hopfield network, connecting the retrieval construction to conditions under which its dynamics settle over time.
summary.tldr: Labeling RAAM encodes cyclic labeled graphs with explicit pointers and supports retrieval by both reference and content.

title: Encoding Labeled Graphs by Labeling RAAM

abstract: Most of the common techniques for estimating conditional prob(cid:173) ability densities are inappropriate for applications involving peri(cid:173) odic variables. In this paper we introduce three novel techniques for tackling such problems, and investigate their performance us(cid:173) ing synthetic data. We then apply these techniques to the problem of extracting the distribution of wind vector directions from radar scatterometer data gathered by a remote-sensing satellite.
originalAbstract: Most of the common techniques for estimating conditional prob(cid:173) ability densities are inappropriate for applications involving peri(cid:173) odic variables. In this paper we introduce three novel techniques for tackling such problems, and investigate their performance us(cid:173) ing synthetic data. We then apply these techniques to the problem of extracting the distribution of wind vector directions from radar scatterometer data gathered by a remote-sensing satellite.

paragraphs: This paper addresses probability estimation for variables that wrap around, such as directions. A periodic variable returns to the same value after a full cycle, so values on opposite sides of a numerical boundary can describe nearby outcomes. The authors argue that many common methods for estimating conditional probability densities are unsuitable for this structure.

They introduce three techniques designed for periodic variables and investigate them using synthetic data. The target is a conditional distribution: a description of which outcomes are plausible given particular observations. Estimating an entire distribution allows the method to express uncertainty about direction while respecting the circular nature of the quantity being predicted.

The techniques are then applied to wind-direction distributions inferred from radar scatterometer measurements collected by a remote-sensing satellite. This application connects the methodological issue to a concrete sensing problem, where observations must be translated into possible directions. The contribution is a set of approaches that explicitly accommodate periodic outcomes, together with synthetic-data evaluation and an application to satellite-based wind inference.
summary.tldr: Three conditional-density estimation techniques handle periodic variables and are applied to inferring wind-direction distributions from satellite radar data.

title: Estimating Conditional Probability Densities for Periodic Variables

abstract: We seek to analyze and manipulate two factors, which we call style and content, underlying a set of observations. We fit training data with bilinear models which explicitly represent the two-factor struc(cid:173) ture. These models can adapt easily during testing to new styles or content, allowing us to solve three general tasks: extrapolation of a new style to unobserved content; classification of content observed in a new style; and translation of new content observed in a new style. For classification, we embed bilinear models in a probabilistic framework, Separable Mixture Models (SMMsj, which generalizes earlier work on factorial mixture models [7, 3]. Significant per(cid:173) formance improvement on a benchmark speech dataset shows the benefits of our approach.
originalAbstract: We seek to analyze and manipulate two factors, which we call style and content, underlying a set of observations. We fit training data with bilinear models which explicitly represent the two-factor struc(cid:173) ture. These models can adapt easily during testing to new styles or content, allowing us to solve three general tasks: extrapolation of a new style to unobserved content; classification of content observed in a new style; and translation of new content observed in a new style. For classification, we embed bilinear models in a probabilistic framework, Separable Mixture Models (SMMsj, which generalizes earlier work on factorial mixture models [7, 3]. Significant per(cid:173) formance improvement on a benchmark speech dataset shows the benefits of our approach.

paragraphs: The paper models observations as the interaction of two underlying factors, called style and content. Its aim is to analyze and manipulate these factors separately. The authors fit bilinear models that explicitly encode the two-factor structure, allowing the representation to adapt at test time when style or content changes.

This supports three tasks. A new style can be extended to content that has not been observed in that style. Content can be classified when it appears in an unfamiliar style. New content observed in a new style can also be translated. These tasks share a requirement to separate what is represented from the way it appears.

For classification, the authors place the bilinear models within a probabilistic framework called Separable Mixture Models, extending earlier factorial mixture models. They report significant performance improvement on a benchmark speech dataset. The finding supports the usefulness of explicitly representing the two factors when classification must accommodate stylistic variation, while the broader framework also provides ways to adapt and manipulate observations.
summary.tldr: Bilinear models separate style from content, enabling adaptation and manipulation while improving classification on a speech benchmark.

title: Separating Style and Content

abstract: We describe Maximum-Likelihood Continuity Mapping (MALCOM), an alternative to hidden Markov models (HMMs) for processing sequence data such as speech. While HMMs have a discrete "hidden" space con(cid:173) strained by a fixed finite-automaton architecture, MALCOM has a con(cid:173) tinuous hidden space-a continuity map-that is constrained only by a smoothness requirement on paths through the space. MALCOM fits into the same probabilistic framework for speech recognition as HMMs, but it represents a more realistic model of the speech production process. To evaluate the extent to which MALCOM captures speech production information, we generated continuous speech continuity maps for three speakers and used the paths through them to predict measured speech articulator data. The median correlation between the MALCOM paths obtained from only the speech acoustics and articulator measurements was 0.77 on an independent test set not used to train MALCOM or the predictor. This unsupervised model achieved correlations over speak(cid:173) ers and articulators only 0.02 to 0.15 lower than those obtained using an analogous supervised method which used articulatory measurements as well as acoustics ..

paragraphs: MALCOM is a probabilistic model for sequences such as speech. It replaces the discrete hidden space and fixed finite-automaton architecture of a hidden Markov model with a continuous hidden space. Paths through this space must be smooth. The authors present this continuity constraint as a more realistic way to represent the speech production process within a compatible probabilistic recognition framework.

To assess whether the representation captures production information, the authors construct continuity maps for continuous speech from three speakers. They use paths inferred from speech acoustics to predict measured articulator data. On an independent test set used to train neither MALCOM nor the predictor, the median correlation between predictions from these paths and articulator measurements is 0.77.

Across speakers and articulators, correlations are only 0.02 to 0.15 below an analogous supervised method that uses articulator measurements as well as acoustics. These results support the presence of speech-production information in the acoustically learned representation. The evaluation concerns the relationship to articulator measurements, supplying evidence for the model's proposed hidden-space interpretation.
summary.tldr: MALCOM learns smooth continuous speech representations whose paths predict articulator measurements with a median test correlation of 0.77.

title: Maximum-Likelihood Continuity Mapping (MALCOM): An Alternative to HMMs

abstract: There exist many approaches to clustering, but the important issue of feature selection, i.e., selecting the data attributes that are relevant for clustering, is rarely addressed. Feature selection for clustering is difﬁcult due to the absence of class labels. We propose two approaches to feature selection in the context of Gaussian mixture-based clustering. In the ﬁrst one, instead of making hard selections, we estimate feature saliencies. An expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm is derived for this task. The second approach extends Koller and Sahami’s mutual-information- based feature relevance criterion to the unsupervised case. Feature selec- tion is then carried out by a backward search scheme. This scheme can be classiﬁed as a “wrapper”, since it wraps mixture estimation in an outer layer that performs feature selection. Experimental results on synthetic and real data show that both methods have promising performance.
originalAbstract: There exist many approaches to clustering, but the important issue of feature selection, i.e., selecting the data attributes that are relevant for clustering, is rarely addressed. Feature selection for clustering is difﬁcult due to the absence of class labels. We propose two approaches to feature selection in the context of Gaussian mixture-based clustering. In the ﬁrst one, instead of making hard selections, we estimate feature saliencies. An expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm is derived for this task. The second approach extends Koller and Sahami’s mutual-information- based feature relevance criterion to the unsupervised case. Feature selec- tion is then carried out by a backward search scheme. This scheme can be classiﬁed as a “wrapper”, since it wraps mixture estimation in an outer layer that performs feature selection. Experimental results on synthetic and real data show that both methods have promising performance.

paragraphs: Selecting useful attributes for clustering is difficult because there are no class labels to indicate which distinctions matter. This paper addresses that problem within Gaussian mixture clustering. It proposes two ways to assess feature relevance while learning groups from the data, making the choice of attributes part of the unsupervised modeling process.

The first approach estimates feature saliencies rather than immediately making binary include-or-exclude decisions. The authors derive an expectation-maximization algorithm for this estimation. This gives the model a way to express degrees of relevance, allowing the treatment of features to be learned alongside the mixture-based account of the data.

The second approach extends a mutual-information relevance criterion to the unsupervised setting and uses backward search to select features. It is a wrapper method: an outer feature-selection procedure surrounds mixture estimation. Experiments on synthetic and real data show promising performance for both approaches. Together, the methods offer two distinct routes to the same objective—estimating relevance within the model or searching over feature choices around it.
summary.tldr: Two methods select useful clustering features through EM-based saliency estimation or a mutual-information wrapper around Gaussian mixture fitting.

title: Feature Selection in Mixture-Based Clustering

abstract: Standard approaches to object detection focus on local patches of the image, and try to classify them as background or not. We propose to use the scene context (image as a whole) as an extra source of (global) information, to help resolve local ambiguities. We present a conditional random ﬁeld for jointly solving the tasks of object detection and scene classiﬁcation.
originalAbstract: Standard approaches to object detection focus on local patches of the image, and try to classify them as background or not. We propose to use the scene context (image as a whole) as an extra source of (global) information, to help resolve local ambiguities. We present a conditional random ﬁeld for jointly solving the tasks of object detection and scene classiﬁcation.

paragraphs: The paper addresses ambiguity in object detection from image patches. A local region may not provide enough information to decide whether it belongs to the background or contains an object. The authors propose using the image’s overall scene as an additional source of evidence for interpreting those local regions.

Their model is a conditional random field that handles object detection and scene classification jointly. This links two levels of image understanding: identifying objects within parts of the image and classifying the image as a scene. Putting both tasks in one model gives global context a role in the local detection problem.

The stated contribution is this joint formulation and its use of scene information to help resolve local ambiguity. Its importance lies in making the relationship between whole-image interpretation and object-level decisions explicit within a graphical model. A patch is therefore interpreted with access to information about the larger scene, which is the additional source of evidence the paper proposes to exploit.
summary.tldr: A conditional random field jointly models object detection and scene classification so that global image context can help resolve local ambiguities.

title: Using the Forest to See the Trees: A Graphical Model Relating Features, Objects, and Scenes

abstract: We describe a system that localizes a single dipole to reasonable accu- racy from noisy magnetoencephalographic (MEG) measurements in real time. At its core is a multilayer perceptron (MLP) trained to map sen- sor signals and head position to dipole location. Including head position overcomes the previous need to retrain the MLP for each subject and ses- sion. The training dataset was generated by mapping randomly chosen dipoles and head positions through an analytic model and adding noise from real MEG recordings. After training, a localization took 0.7 ms with an average error of 0.90 cm. A few iterations of a Levenberg-Marquardt routine using the MLP’s output as its initial guess took 15 ms and im- proved the accuracy to 0.53 cm, only slightly above the statistical limits on accuracy imposed by the noise. We applied these methods to localize single dipole sources from MEG components isolated by blind source separation and compared the estimated locations to those generated by standard manually-assisted commercial software.

paragraphs: This paper presents a system for rapidly locating a single dipole source from noisy MEG measurements. A multilayer perceptron maps sensor signals and head position to a source location. Including head position addresses the previous need to retrain the network for each subject and recording session.

Training examples are generated by passing randomly selected dipoles and head positions through an analytic model, then adding noise from real MEG recordings. After training, the network produces a location in 0.7 milliseconds with an average error of 0.90 centimeters. This provides a fast initial estimate using both the measured signals and the head's position.

A few Levenberg-Marquardt iterations initialized with the network estimate take 15 milliseconds and reduce the error to 0.53 centimeters, slightly above the noise-imposed statistical accuracy limit. The authors also apply the methods to single-dipole MEG components isolated by blind source separation and compare locations with manually assisted commercial software. The approach offers rapid direct localization and a more accurate refinement option within the single-dipole setting.
summary.tldr: A neural network incorporating head position localizes single MEG dipoles rapidly across subjects, with iterative refinement improving accuracy.

title: Subject-Independent Magnetoencephalographic Source Localization by a Multilayer Perceptron

abstract: We propose a convex optimization based strategy to deal with uncertainty in the observations of a classification problem. We assume that instead of a sample (xi, yi) a distribution over (xi, yi) is specified. In particu- lar, we derive a robust formulation when the distribution is given by a normal distribution. It leads to Second Order Cone Programming formu- lation. Our method is applied to the problem of missing data, where it outperforms direct imputation.
originalAbstract: We propose a convex optimization based strategy to deal with uncertainty in the observations of a classification problem. We assume that instead of a sample (xi, yi) a distribution over (xi, yi) is specified. In particu- lar, we derive a robust formulation when the distribution is given by a normal distribution. It leads to Second Order Cone Programming formu- lation. Our method is applied to the problem of missing data, where it outperforms direct imputation.

paragraphs: This paper approaches classification when observations are uncertain, including situations with missing data. Its starting assumption is that a distribution is provided over each input-label pair instead of a single fully specified example. The learning problem therefore receives uncertainty as part of the description of the observations.

For normally distributed uncertainty, the authors derive a robust classification formulation that becomes a second-order cone program. This places the treatment of uncertainty inside a convex optimization problem. The normal-distribution assumption is the stated basis for the particular robust formulation, linking the probabilistic description of each observation to the mathematical form of training.

The method is applied to missing-data classification and outperforms direct imputation in the reported application. This result supports incorporating uncertainty into the classifier’s optimization when handling incomplete observations. The central contribution is the connection between distribution-valued training examples and a convex classification formulation, with the missing-data application showing a practical benefit relative to directly filling in missing values.
summary.tldr: A robust classifier models uncertain examples as distributions and outperforms direct imputation in a missing-data application.

title: A Second Order Cone programming Formulation for Classifying Missing Data

abstract: We propose a sequential information maximization model as a general strategy for programming eye movements. The model reconstructs high-resolution visual information from a sequence of fixations, taking into account the fall-off in resolution from the fovea to the periphery. From this framework we get a simple rule for predicting fixation sequences: after each fixation, fixate next at the location that minimizes uncertainty (maximizes information) about the stimulus. By comparing our model performance to human eye movement data and to predictions from a saliency and random model, we demonstrate that our model is best at predicting fixation locations. Modeling additional biological constraints will improve the prediction of fixation sequences. Our results suggest that information maximization is a useful principle for programming eye movements.
originalAbstract: We propose a sequential information maximization model as a general strategy for programming eye movements. The model reconstructs high-resolution visual information from a sequence of fixations, taking into account the fall-off in resolution from the fovea to the periphery. From this framework we get a simple rule for predicting fixation sequences: after each fixation, fixate next at the location that minimizes uncertainty (maximizes information) about the stimulus. By comparing our model performance to human eye movement data and to predictions from a saliency and random model, we demonstrate that our model is best at predicting fixation locations. Modeling additional biological constraints will improve the prediction of fixation sequences. Our results suggest that information maximization is a useful principle for programming eye movements.

paragraphs: Human vision gathers detailed information through successive eye fixations because resolution falls away from the fovea. This paper models where to look next as an information-gathering decision. Each fixation should reduce uncertainty about the stimulus given what has already been seen.

The model reconstructs high-resolution visual information across a sequence of fixations while accounting for poorer peripheral resolution. After each observation, it chooses the next location expected to provide the most information. This makes the fixation sequence depend on accumulated knowledge, not just on a fixed map of visually salient locations.

Compared with human eye-movement data, the model predicts fixation locations better than the tested saliency and random alternatives. The authors identify additional biological constraints as a route to improving sequence predictions further. The contribution supports information maximization as a useful organizing principle for active vision, connecting sensory limitations to purposeful selection of the next observation.
summary.tldr: An uncertainty-reduction model predicts human fixation locations better than the compared saliency and random strategies.

title: An Information Maximization Model of Eye Movements

abstract: We formulate the problem of graph inference where part of the graph is known as a supervised learning problem, and propose an algorithm to solve it. The method involves the learning of a mapping of the vertices to a Euclidean space where the graph is easy to infer, and can be formu- lated as an optimization problem in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We report encouraging results on the problem of metabolic network re- construction from genomic data.
originalAbstract: We formulate the problem of graph inference where part of the graph is known as a supervised learning problem, and propose an algorithm to solve it. The method involves the learning of a mapping of the vertices to a Euclidean space where the graph is easy to infer, and can be formu- lated as an optimization problem in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We report encouraging results on the problem of metabolic network re- construction from genomic data.

paragraphs: The paper considers how to infer a graph when part of its structure is already known. It formulates that task as supervised learning, using the available graph information to guide inference of the remaining structure. The central goal is to learn from known relationships rather than treat the whole graph as equally unknown.

Its method learns a mapping from vertices into a Euclidean space where the graph becomes easier to infer. This makes the representation of the vertices part of the learning problem. The authors formulate the task as optimization in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, providing a mathematical framework for learning that mapping from the available supervision.

The approach is applied to reconstructing metabolic networks from genomic data, with encouraging reported results. This supplies an application of the graph-learning formulation rather than a universal claim about reconstruction accuracy. The contribution brings together partial graph knowledge, a learned geometric representation of vertices, and a supervised optimization approach for inferring additional graph structure.
summary.tldr: The paper learns a geometric representation from a partially known graph to support supervised graph inference, with encouraging metabolic-network reconstruction results.

title: Supervised Graph Inference

abstract: We consider the problem of constructing an aggregated estimator from a ﬁnite class of base functions which approximately minimizes a con- vex risk functional under the ℓ1 constraint. For this purpose, we propose a stochastic procedure, the mirror descent, which performs gradient de- scent in the dual space. The generated estimates are additionally aver- aged in a recursive fashion with speciﬁc weights. Mirror descent algo- rithms have been developed in different contexts and they are known to be particularly efﬁcient in high dimensional problems. Moreover their implementation is adapted to the online setting. The main result of the paper is the upper bound on the convergence rate for the generalization error.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of constructing an aggregated estimator from a ﬁnite class of base functions which approximately minimizes a con- vex risk functional under the ℓ1 constraint. For this purpose, we propose a stochastic procedure, the mirror descent, which performs gradient de- scent in the dual space. The generated estimates are additionally aver- aged in a recursive fashion with speciﬁc weights. Mirror descent algo- rithms have been developed in different contexts and they are known to be particularly efﬁcient in high dimensional problems. Moreover their implementation is adapted to the online setting. The main result of the paper is the upper bound on the convergence rate for the generalization error.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to combine a finite collection of base functions into an estimator with low risk. Its objective is to approximately minimize a convex risk functional under an ℓ1 constraint, which restricts the aggregate's coefficients through their absolute magnitudes. The challenge is to construct the combination and control its generalization error.

The proposed procedure uses stochastic mirror descent, carrying out gradient descent in a dual space. The estimates produced along the way are additionally combined through recursive averaging with specific weights. Both the optimization updates and this averaging step belong to the proposed construction, rather than the final estimator being simply one unaveraged update.

The main result is an upper bound on the convergence rate of the generalization error. This supplies theoretical control over how the aggregate approaches the desired risk objective. The abstract also highlights mirror descent's suitability for high-dimensional problems and online implementation. The contribution is thus an aggregation procedure with a generalization guarantee, built from a method that can accommodate sequential learning.
summary.tldr: Stochastic mirror descent with weighted recursive averaging constructs constrained aggregates with an upper bound on generalization-error convergence.

title: Generalization Error Bounds for Aggregation by Mirror Descent with Averaging

abstract: We describe a hierarchy of motif-based kernels for multiple alignments of biological sequences, particularly suitable to process regulatory regions of genes. The kernels incorporate progressively more information, with the most complex kernel accounting for a multiple alignment of orthologous regions, the phylogenetic tree relating the species, and the prior knowledge that relevant sequence patterns occur in conserved motif blocks. These kernels can be used in the presence of a library of known transcription factor binding sites, or de novo by iterating over all k -mers of a given length. In the latter mode, a discriminative classifier built from such a kernel not only recognizes a given class of promoter regions, but as a side effect simultaneously identifies a collection of relevant, discriminative sequence motifs. We demonstrate the utility of the motif-based multiple alignment kernels by using a collection of aligned promoter regions from five yeast species to recognize classes of cell-cycle regulated genes. Supplementary data is available at http://noble.gs.washington.edu/proj/pkernel.

paragraphs: The paper develops a hierarchy of kernels for comparing multiple alignments of biological sequences, particularly gene regulatory regions. The comparisons are based on sequence motifs. Successively richer kernels incorporate more biological information, allowing the representation to reflect more than isolated sequence patterns.

The most detailed kernel accounts for aligned orthologous regions, the evolutionary tree connecting species, and prior knowledge that relevant patterns occur in conserved motif blocks. The kernels can use a library of known transcription factor binding sites. Alternatively, they can work de novo by considering all sequence fragments of a chosen length.

In the de novo setting, a discriminative classifier performs two related functions: recognizing a class of promoter regions and identifying motifs that help distinguish that class. The authors demonstrate the approach using aligned promoter regions from five yeast species to recognize classes of genes regulated during the cell cycle. The contribution is a way to combine motif information, cross-species alignment, and evolutionary relationships within a classification framework that can also reveal discriminative sequence patterns.
summary.tldr: Motif-based kernels combine aligned regulatory sequences and evolutionary information to classify promoter regions and identify discriminative motifs.

title: Kernels for gene regulatory regions

abstract: We introduce Coherent Point Drift (CPD), a novel probabilistic method for nonrigid registration of point sets. The registration is treated as a Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation problem with motion coherence constraint over the velocity field such that one point set moves coherently to align with the second set. We formulate the motion coherence constraint and derive a solution of regularized ML estimation through the variational approach, which leads to an elegant kernel form. We also derive the EM algorithm for the penalized ML optimization with deterministic annealing. The CPD method simultaneously finds both the non-rigid transformation and the correspondence between two point sets without making any prior assumption of the transformation model except that of motion coherence. This method can estimate complex non-linear non-rigid transformations, and is shown to be accurate on 2D and 3D examples and robust in the presence of outliers and missing points.
originalAbstract: We introduce Coherent Point Drift (CPD), a novel probabilistic method for nonrigid registration of point sets. The registration is treated as a Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation problem with motion coherence constraint over the velocity field such that one point set moves coherently to align with the second set. We formulate the motion coherence constraint and derive a solution of regularized ML estimation through the variational approach, which leads to an elegant kernel form. We also derive the EM algorithm for the penalized ML optimization with deterministic annealing. The CPD method simultaneously finds both the non-rigid transformation and the correspondence between two point sets without making any prior assumption of the transformation model except that of motion coherence. This method can estimate complex non-linear non-rigid transformations, and is shown to be accurate on 2D and 3D examples and robust in the presence of outliers and missing points.

paragraphs: Coherent Point Drift aligns two point sets when one may need to deform nonrigidly to match the other. The paper treats alignment as a maximum-likelihood estimation problem and imposes motion coherence on the velocity field. This constraint makes the movement of the points coherent while allowing a complex deformation.

The authors formulate that constraint and derive a regularized maximum-likelihood solution using a variational approach, obtaining a kernel representation. They also derive an expectation-maximization algorithm with deterministic annealing for the penalized optimization. The procedure estimates the transformation and the correspondence between the point sets together, so those two unknowns are resolved within the same probabilistic framework.

The stated transformation assumption is motion coherence; the method does not require an additional predefined transformation model. It can estimate complex nonlinear, nonrigid transformations. Examples in two and three dimensions demonstrate accurate alignment and robustness to outliers and missing points. These results show how the coherence constraint can guide flexible deformation while jointly recovering which points correspond.
summary.tldr: Coherent Point Drift jointly estimates point correspondences and nonrigid deformation using probabilistic fitting constrained by coherent motion.

title: Non-rigid point set registration: Coherent Point Drift

abstract: We consider how a search engine should select advertisements to display with search results, in order to maximize its revenue. Under the standard "pay-per-click" arrangement, revenue depends on how well the displayed advertisements appeal to users. The main difficulty stems from new advertisements whose degree of appeal has yet to be determined. Often the only reliable way of determining appeal is exploration via display to users, which detracts from exploitation of other advertisements known to have high appeal. Budget constraints and finite advertisement lifetimes make it necessary to explore as well as exploit. In this paper we study the tradeoff between exploration and exploitation, modeling advertisement placement as a multi-armed bandit problem. We extend traditional bandit formulations to account for budget constraints that occur in search engine advertising markets, and derive theoretical bounds on the performance of a family of algorithms. We measure empirical performance via extensive experiments over real-world data.

paragraphs: A search engine earning money from clicks must choose between displaying ads known to appeal to users and testing new ads whose appeal is uncertain. Testing can reveal valuable information, but it takes display opportunities away from established ads. This paper studies that exploration-versus-exploitation tradeoff with revenue as the objective.

The authors model advertisement placement as a multi-armed bandit problem. They extend traditional bandit formulations to incorporate advertiser budget constraints. The motivation also includes finite advertisement lifetimes: both budgets and limited availability make it necessary to consider learning about new ads alongside earning revenue from currently promising ones.

The paper derives theoretical performance bounds for a family of algorithms and evaluates empirical performance through extensive experiments on real-world data. These contributions address two complementary questions: what guarantees can be established within the model, and how the algorithms behave on observed advertising data. The supplied abstract reports the evaluation without specifying a winning algorithm or numerical gains. The main contribution is bringing market constraints into the sequential decision problem.
summary.tldr: The paper models search-ad selection as a budget-constrained bandit problem and develops performance bounds and empirical evaluations for algorithms balancing exploration and revenue.

title: Handling Advertisements of Unknown Quality in Search Advertising

abstract: Cooperative competitive networks are believed to play a central role in cortical processing and have been shown to exhibit a wide set of useful computational properties. We propose a VLSI implementation of a spiking cooperative competitive network and show how it can perform context dependent computation both in the mean firing rate domain and in spike timing correlation space. In the mean rate case the network amplifies the activity of neurons belonging to the selected stimulus and suppresses the activity of neurons receiving weaker stimuli. In the event correlation case, the recurrent network amplifies with a higher gain the correlation between neurons which receive highly correlated inputs while leaving the mean firing rate unaltered. We describe the network architecture and present experimental data demonstrating its context dependent computation capabilities.

paragraphs: Cooperative competitive networks combine interactions that strengthen some activity patterns and suppress others. This paper implements such a network with spiking neurons in VLSI hardware. It investigates context-dependent computation in two different aspects of the spikes: how frequently neurons fire and how closely their firing events are correlated in time.

For average firing rates, the network strengthens activity associated with a selected stimulus and suppresses neurons receiving weaker stimuli. This provides a form of selection expressed through the amount of activity. The experimental demonstration connects the network's cooperative and competitive organization to a measurable response to competing inputs.

The timing result concerns a different signal property. Through recurrent interactions, the network gives greater amplification to correlations among neurons receiving highly correlated inputs, while leaving the mean firing rate unchanged. The authors describe the architecture and present experimental evidence for both behaviors. Together, the findings show that context-dependent processing in this hardware can operate through either firing rates or relationships among spike times.
summary.tldr: A spiking hardware network selectively amplifies firing rates or spike-time correlations, with correlation amplification leaving mean rates unchanged.

title: Context dependent amplification of both rate and event-correlation in a VLSI network of spiking neurons

abstract: We present a novel message passing algorithm for approximating the MAP problem in graphical models. The algorithm is similar in structure to max-product but unlike max-product it always converges, and can be proven to find the exact MAP solution in various settings. The algorithm is derived via block coordinate descent in a dual of the LP relaxation of MAP, but does not require any tunable parameters such as step size or tree weights. We also describe a generalization of the method to cluster based potentials. The new method is tested on synthetic and real-world problems, and compares favorably with previous approaches.

paragraphs: Finding a graphical model's most probable joint assignment is the MAP inference problem. This paper introduces an approximation algorithm with a message-passing structure similar to max-product. Its distinguishing property is that it always converges, addressing a central difficulty with using max-product as a dependable inference procedure.

The algorithm comes from block coordinate descent applied to a dual formulation of a linear programming relaxation of MAP. In practical terms, its message updates follow an optimization construction rather than requiring a manually chosen step size or tree weights. The paper also extends the approach to cluster-based potentials, broadening the kinds of interactions that the method can represent.

Convergence and exactness are separate claims here. The method always converges, while recovery of the exact MAP solution is proved for various settings. Tests on synthetic and real-world problems compare favorably with previous approaches. The contribution combines an explicit optimization foundation, freedom from the listed tuning parameters, and empirical evidence of useful inference performance.
summary.tldr: An optimization-derived message-passing algorithm always converges and provably recovers exact MAP solutions in various settings without step-size or tree-weight tuning.

title: Fixing Max-Product: Convergent Message Passing Algorithms for MAP LP-Relaxations

abstract: We study the behavior of the popular Laplacian Regularization method for Semi-Supervised Learning at the regime of a fixed number of labeled points but a large number of unlabeled points. We show that in $\R^d$, $d \geq 2$, the method is actually not well-posed, and as the number of unlabeled points increases the solution degenerates to a noninformative function. We also contrast the method with the Laplacian Eigenvector method, and discuss the ``smoothness assumptions associated with this alternate method.

We show that in $\R^d$, $d \geq 2$, the method is actually not well-posed, and as the number of unlabeled points increases the solution degenerates to a noninformative function. We also contrast the method with the Laplacian Eigenvector method, and discuss the ``smoothness assumptions associated with this alternate method.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning attempts to use unlabeled examples alongside labeled ones. This paper examines a specific asymptotic setting for Laplacian regularization: the number of labeled points stays fixed while the number of unlabeled points becomes large. The question is whether adding more unlabeled data preserves an informative solution under those conditions.

The authors show that, in Euclidean spaces of dimension at least two, the method is not well-posed in this regime. As unlabeled points accumulate, its solution degenerates into a noninformative function. The finding identifies a failure of this particular method and limiting setup; it does not establish that unlabeled data is generally harmful or that all semi-supervised procedures fail.

The paper also contrasts Laplacian regularization with the Laplacian eigenvector method and discusses the smoothness assumptions associated with that alternative. This comparison emphasizes that methods drawing on related mathematical ideas can rely on different assumptions about the function being learned. The main lesson is that the balance between fixed supervision and increasingly abundant unlabeled data requires analysis, rather than an automatic expectation of improvement.
summary.tldr: With fixed labeled data, Laplacian regularization degenerates as unlabeled data grows in Euclidean dimensions of at least two.

title: Statistical Analysis of Semi-Supervised Learning: The Limit of Infinite Unlabelled Data

abstract: High dimensional time series are endemic in applications of machine learning such as robotics (sensor data), computational biology (gene expression data), vision (video sequences) and graphics (motion capture data). Practical nonlinear probabilistic approaches to this data are required. In this paper we introduce the variational Gaussian process dynamical system. Our work builds on recent variational approximations for Gaussian process latent variable models to allow for nonlinear dimensionality reduction simultaneously with learning a dynamical prior in the latent space. The approach also allows for the appropriate dimensionality of the latent space to be automatically determined. We demonstrate the model on a human motion capture data set and a series of high resolution video sequences.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a probabilistic model for high-dimensional time series, where many observed quantities change together over time. Such data arise in sensor streams, gene expression, video, and motion capture. The proposed variational Gaussian process dynamical system aims to describe these observations through a lower-dimensional latent representation while learning their temporal organization.

The method builds on variational approximations for Gaussian process latent-variable models. It performs nonlinear dimensionality reduction at the same time as learning a dynamical prior in the latent space. These two components connect the compact representation of each observation with a model of how the hidden representation varies over time, rather than treating those tasks separately.

The approach also allows the appropriate latent dimensionality to be determined automatically. This makes the size of the hidden representation part of the modeling process. Demonstrations use human motion capture data and high-resolution video sequences, showing applications to two forms of complex temporal data. The contribution is a joint framework for nonlinear representation learning, latent dynamics, and dimensionality determination.
summary.tldr: A variational Gaussian process dynamical system jointly learns nonlinear low-dimensional representations, latent temporal structure, and an appropriate latent dimension.

title: Variational Gaussian Process Dynamical Systems

abstract: The human mind has a remarkable ability to store a vast amount of information in memory, and an even more remarkable ability to retrieve these experiences when needed. Understanding the representations and algorithms that underlie human memory search could potentially be useful in other information retrieval settings, including internet search. Psychological studies have revealed clear regularities in how people search their memory, with clusters of semantically related items tending to be retrieved together. These findings have recently been taken as evidence that human memory search is similar to animals foraging for food in patchy environments, with people making a rational decision to switch away from a cluster of related information as it becomes depleted. We demonstrate that the results that were taken as evidence for this account also emerge from a random walk on a semantic network, much like the random web surfer model used in internet search engines. This offers a simpler and more unified account of how people search their memory, postulating a single process rather than one process for exploring a cluster and one process for switching between clusters.

paragraphs: When people search memory, related items tend to appear together in clusters. One explanation compares this behavior to animals searching for food in patches: people explore a group of related memories, then decide to leave as that group becomes depleted. This account assigns separate roles to searching within a cluster and switching between clusters.

The paper shows that the findings used to support that explanation also arise from a random walk on a semantic network. In this alternative, retrieval follows links between related items through a single process. The network’s organization allows clustered retrieval and movement between clusters to emerge without adding a separate rational switching decision.

The result offers a simpler, unified account of the observed memory-search patterns. It shows that those patterns can be explained by more than one underlying mechanism. The authors also connect the model conceptually to the random web surfer used in internet search, suggesting that studying memory representations and retrieval processes could potentially inform other information-retrieval settings.
summary.tldr: A random walk through a semantic network reproduces memory-search patterns previously attributed to separate exploration and switching processes.

title: Human memory search as a random walk in a semantic network

abstract: For modeling data matrices, this paper introduces Probabilistic Co-Subspace Addition (PCSA) model by simultaneously capturing the dependent structures among both rows and columns. Briefly, PCSA assumes that each entry of a matrix is generated by the additive combination of the linear mappings of two features, which distribute in the row-wise and column-wise latent subspaces. Consequently, it captures the dependencies among entries intricately, and is able to model the non-Gaussian and heteroscedastic density. Variational inference is proposed on PCSA for approximate Bayesian learning, where the updating for posteriors is formulated into the problem of solving Sylvester equations. Furthermore, PCSA is extended to tackling and filling missing values, to adapting its sparseness, and to modelling tensor data. In comparison with several state-of-art approaches, experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of Bayesian (sparse) PCSA on modeling matrix (tensor) data and filling missing values.

paragraphs: Probabilistic Co-Subspace Addition, or PCSA, models a data matrix by capturing dependencies along both its rows and its columns. It assumes that each entry combines two contributions additively: linear mappings of features from a row-related latent subspace and a column-related latent subspace. Both directions therefore participate in explaining individual entries.

This construction can represent intricate dependencies, non-Gaussian densities, and heteroscedasticity, meaning variability that is not constant across the data. For approximate Bayesian learning, the authors develop variational inference in which posterior updates become problems involving Sylvester equations. The probabilistic representation and its inference procedure together form the core method.

The paper also extends PCSA to fill missing values, adapt its sparsity, and model tensor data. Experiments against several existing approaches demonstrate effectiveness and efficiency for matrix and tensor modeling and for missing-value completion. These results support treating row and column structure jointly through additive latent contributions, with extensions that broaden the types of incomplete and multidimensional data the method can address.
summary.tldr: PCSA models matrix entries through additive row and column latent features, with Bayesian extensions for sparsity, missing values, and tensors.

title: Bayesian Probabilistic Co-Subspace Addition

abstract: We consider the problem of embedding entities and relationships of multi-relational data in low-dimensional vector spaces. Our objective is to propose a canonical model which is easy to train, contains a reduced number of parameters and can scale up to very large databases. Hence, we propose, TransE, a method which models relationships by interpreting them as translations operating on the low-dimensional embeddings of the entities. Despite its simplicity, this assumption proves to be powerful since extensive experiments show that TransE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in link prediction on two knowledge bases. Besides, it can be successfully trained on a large scale data set with 1M entities, 25k relationships and more than 17M training samples.

paragraphs: Multi-relational data describe entities connected by different kinds of relationships. This paper introduces TransE, a model that represents entities and relations in a low-dimensional vector space. Its design aims for easy training, a small parameter count, and the ability to handle very large databases.

The central assumption is that a relationship acts as a translation between entity embeddings. In geometric terms, applying the relation's displacement to one entity's representation should bring it toward the representation of the related entity. This gives different relations a common, simple mathematical form while allowing each to express a different displacement in the learned space.

Despite that simplicity, experiments on two knowledge bases show significant link-prediction improvements over leading comparison methods. The authors also successfully train the model on a dataset containing one million entities, 25,000 relationships, and more than 17 million training examples. These findings support both the predictive usefulness of the translation assumption in the evaluated settings and the model's ability to train at large scale.
summary.tldr: TransE models relations as vector translations, improving link prediction on two knowledge bases while supporting million-entity training.

title: Translating Embeddings for Modeling Multi-relational Data

abstract: Learning a visual concept from a small number of positive examples is a significant challenge for machine learning algorithms. Current methods typically fail to find the appropriate level of generalization in a concept hierarchy for a given set of visual examples. Recent work in cognitive science on Bayesian models of generalization addresses this challenge, but prior results assumed that objects were perfectly recognized. We present an algorithm for learning visual concepts directly from images, using probabilistic predictions generated by visual classifiers as the input to a Bayesian generalization model. As no existing challenge data tests this paradigm, we collect and make available a new, large-scale dataset for visual concept learning using the ImageNet hierarchy as the source of possible concepts, with human annotators to provide ground truth labels as to whether a new image is an instance of each concept using a paradigm similar to that used in experiments studying word learning in children. We compare the performance of our system to several baseline algorithms, and show a significant advantage results from combining visual classifiers with the ability to identify an appropriate level of abstraction using Bayesian generalization.

paragraphs: Learning a visual concept from a few positive examples requires deciding how broadly those examples should generalize. A concept hierarchy offers several possible levels of abstraction, and choosing the right one is difficult. Earlier Bayesian accounts addressed generalization while assuming that the objects in the examples had been recognized perfectly.

This paper connects visual recognition to Bayesian generalization directly. Probabilistic outputs from visual classifiers become the input to the generalization model, allowing it to work from images rather than perfect object labels. The design combines uncertainty about visual recognition with the task of identifying an appropriate level in the concept hierarchy.

The authors also create and release a large-scale dataset because existing challenges did not test this combination. It uses the ImageNet hierarchy for candidate concepts and human judgments about whether new images belong to them, following a paradigm related to studies of children's word learning. Comparisons with several baseline algorithms show a significant advantage from combining visual classifiers with Bayesian selection of the abstraction level, supporting the value of treating recognition and generalization together.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic visual recognition combined with Bayesian generalization helps learn the appropriate concept breadth from a few positive images.

title: Visual Concept Learning: Combining Machine Vision and Bayesian Generalization on Concept Hierarchies

abstract: We introduce a new objective function for pool-based Bayesian active learning with probabilistic hypotheses. This objective function, called the policy Gibbs error, is the expected error rate of a random classifier drawn from the prior distribution on the examples adaptively selected by the active learning policy. Exact maximization of the policy Gibbs error is hard, so we propose a greedy strategy that maximizes the Gibbs error at each iteration, where the Gibbs error on an instance is the expected error of a random classifier selected from the posterior label distribution on that instance. We apply this maximum Gibbs error criterion to three active learning scenarios: non-adaptive, adaptive, and batch active learning. In each scenario, we prove that the criterion achieves near-maximal policy Gibbs error when constrained to a fixed budget. For practical implementations, we provide approximations to the maximum Gibbs error criterion for Bayesian conditional random fields and transductive Naive Bayes. Our experimental results on a named entity recognition task and a text classification task show that the maximum Gibbs error criterion is an effective active learning criterion for noisy models.

paragraphs: Pool-based active learning chooses which available examples should receive labels. This paper introduces an objective for Bayesian models whose hypotheses make probabilistic predictions. Called policy Gibbs error, it measures the expected error of a classifier sampled from the prior on the examples selected by an active learning policy.

Optimizing that entire selection policy exactly is difficult. The proposed alternative makes a greedy choice at each iteration, selecting an example with maximal Gibbs error under its posterior label distribution. The authors analyze this criterion for non-adaptive, adaptive, and batch selection. In each setting, they prove that it achieves nearly the largest policy Gibbs error available under a fixed budget.

For implementation, the paper develops approximations for Bayesian conditional random fields and transductive Naive Bayes. Experiments on named entity recognition and text classification support its effectiveness with noisy models. The theoretical guarantee concerns the proposed selection objective, while the experiments establish its practical usefulness on those tasks; these are distinct forms of support for the approach.
summary.tldr: Greedy maximum Gibbs error selection nearly optimizes a Bayesian active learning objective under a fixed budget and works effectively with noisy models.

title: Active Learning for Probabilistic Hypotheses Using the Maximum Gibbs Error Criterion

abstract: Consider the binary classification problem of predicting a target variable Y from a discrete feature vector X = (X1,...,Xd). When the probability distribution P(X,Y) is known, the optimal classifier, leading to the minimum misclassification rate, is given by the Maximum A-posteriori Probability (MAP) decision rule. However, in practice, estimating the complete joint distribution P(X,Y) is computationally and statistically impossible for large values of d. Therefore, an alternative approach is to first estimate some low order marginals of the joint probability distribution P(X,Y) and then design the classifier based on the estimated low order marginals. This approach is also helpful when the complete training data instances are not available due to privacy concerns. In this work, we consider the problem of designing the optimum classifier based on some estimated low order marginals of (X,Y). We prove that for a given set of marginals, the minimum Hirschfeld-Gebelein-R´enyi (HGR) correlation principle introduced in [1] leads to a randomized classification rule which is shown to have a misclassification rate no larger than twice the misclassification rate of the optimal classifier. Then, we show that under a separability condition, the proposed algorithm is equivalent to a randomized linear regression approach which naturally results in a robust feature selection method selecting a subset of features having the maximum worst case HGR correlation with the target variable. Our theoretical upper-bound is similar to the recent Discrete Chebyshev Classifier (DCC) approach [2], while the proposed algorithm has significant computational advantages since it only requires solving a least square optimization problem. Finally, we numerically compare our proposed algorithm with the DCC classifier and show that the proposed algorithm results in better misclassification rate over various UCI data repository datasets.

paragraphs: For binary classification with many discrete features, estimating the full joint distribution of inputs and labels can be impractical. This paper instead builds a classifier from low-order marginals: distributions involving only small groups of variables. That setting also accommodates situations where privacy concerns prevent access to complete training records.

The proposed method uses a minimum Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Rényi correlation principle to construct a randomized classifier. For the given marginals, the authors prove an error bound no larger than twice the optimal classifier's misclassification rate. Under a separability condition, the method becomes equivalent to randomized linear regression and leads to robust feature selection based on worst-case correlation with the target.

Its theoretical bound resembles that of the Discrete Chebyshev Classifier, while offering computational advantages. Numerical comparisons on several UCI datasets also report lower misclassification rates. The paper therefore combines a worst-case classification guarantee, a conditional connection to regression, and empirical evidence of useful performance.
summary.tldr: A randomized classifier built from low-order marginals offers a factor-two error bound and, under separability, a least-squares regression formulation.

title: Discrete Rényi Classifiers

abstract: This paper studies single-image depth perception in the wild, i.e., recovering depth from a single image taken in unconstrained settings. We introduce a new dataset “Depth in the Wild” consisting of images in the wild annotated with relative depth between pairs of random points. We also propose a new algorithm that learns to estimate metric depth using annotations of relative depth. Compared to the state of the art, our algorithm is simpler and performs better. Experiments show that our algorithm, combined with existing RGB-D data and our new relative depth annotations, significantly improves single-image depth perception in the wild.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to recover depth from a single photograph taken in an unconstrained setting. Its focus is depth perception in ordinary images rather than a narrowly controlled collection. To support that task, the authors introduce Depth in the Wild, a dataset whose images carry relative-depth annotations between randomly chosen pairs of points.

These annotations describe how depths compare at two locations rather than directly supplying a complete metric-depth map. The paper also introduces an algorithm that learns to estimate metric depth using this relative information. This connects a comparatively limited form of supervision with a richer prediction target: the model uses pairwise depth relationships to help learn depth estimates.

The authors report that the algorithm is simpler and performs better than the state of the art they compare against. Experiments combine the new relative-depth annotations with existing RGB-D data and show significant improvements in single-image depth perception in the wild. The result supports the usefulness of both the added supervision and the proposed learning approach.
summary.tldr: Depth in the Wild and a new learning algorithm use relative-depth annotations to improve depth estimation from unconstrained photographs.

title: Single-Image Depth Perception in the Wild

abstract: This work explores CNNs for the recognition of novel categories from few examples. Inspired by the transferability properties of CNNs, we introduce an additional unsupervised meta-training stage that exposes multiple top layer units to a large amount of unlabeled real-world images. By encouraging these units to learn diverse sets of low-density separators across the unlabeled data, we capture a more generic, richer description of the visual world, which decouples these units from ties to a specific set of categories. We propose an unsupervised margin maximization that jointly estimates compact high-density regions and infers low-density separators. The low-density separator (LDS) modules can be plugged into any or all of the top layers of a standard CNN architecture. The resulting CNNs significantly improve the performance in scene classification, fine-grained recognition, and action recognition with small training samples.

paragraphs: The paper asks how convolutional neural networks can recognize new categories from only a few examples. Its approach adds an unsupervised meta-training stage that exposes multiple units in the network's upper layers to many unlabeled real-world images. This stage aims to make those units describe visual structure more broadly than a particular set of training categories.

The method encourages diverse low-density separators: boundaries that pass through sparsely populated parts of the unlabeled data. An unsupervised margin-maximization procedure jointly estimates compact, high-density regions and the separators between them. Learning these two aspects together provides a way to organize visual representations without requiring category labels for the additional images.

The resulting low-density-separator modules can be inserted into any or all upper layers of a standard CNN. The authors report significant improvements in scene classification, fine-grained recognition, and action recognition when training samples are scarce. These findings support unlabeled meta-training as a way to make upper-layer representations more useful for learning unfamiliar categories.
summary.tldr: Unsupervised meta-training teaches CNN upper layers broader visual structure, improving recognition when labeled examples are scarce.

title: Learning from Small Sample Sets by Combining Unsupervised Meta-Training with CNNs

abstract: We propose a class of loss functions, which we call deep perceptual similarity metrics (DeePSiM), allowing to generate sharp high resolution images from compressed abstract representations. Instead of computing distances in the image space, we compute distances between image features extracted by deep neural networks. This metric reflects perceptual similarity of images much better and, thus, leads to better results. We demonstrate two examples of use cases of the proposed loss: (1) networks that invert the AlexNet convolutional network; (2) a modified version of a variational autoencoder that generates realistic high-resolution random images.

paragraphs: Generating an image from a compressed, abstract representation requires a way to judge whether the result resembles the intended image. This paper proposes deep perceptual similarity metrics, or DeePSiM, as a class of training losses for that purpose. The goal is to produce sharp, high-resolution images using a comparison that better reflects visual similarity.

Instead of measuring distance directly in image space, the method compares features extracted from images by deep neural networks. This changes what the training objective treats as a close match. The authors report that the feature-based metric reflects perceptual similarity much better and consequently improves the generated results.

Two demonstrations show how the loss can be used. One trains networks to invert representations from the AlexNet convolutional network. The other modifies a variational autoencoder to generate realistic, high-resolution random images. Together, these applications show that the contribution is a reusable way to evaluate image similarity during learning, with demonstrated uses in both reconstructing images from network representations and generating new images.
summary.tldr: DeePSiM trains image generators by comparing deep-network features, producing sharper images that better preserve perceptual similarity.

title: Generating Images with Perceptual Similarity Metrics based on Deep Networks

abstract: We study reinforcement learning under model misspecification, where we do not have access to the true environment but only to a reasonably close approximation to it. We address this problem by extending the framework of robust MDPs to the model-free Reinforcement Learning setting, where we do not have access to the model parameters, but can only sample states from it. We define robust versions of Q-learning, Sarsa, and TD-learning and prove convergence to an approximately optimal robust policy and approximate value function respectively. We scale up the robust algorithms to large MDPs via function approximation and prove convergence under two different settings. We prove convergence of robust approximate policy iteration and robust approximate value iteration for linear architectures (under mild assumptions). We also define a robust loss function, the mean squared robust projected Bellman error and give stochastic gradient descent algorithms that are guaranteed to converge to a local minimum.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning when the true environment is unavailable and learning relies on a reasonably close approximation. This mismatch matters because decisions are learned from an environment that does not exactly match the target. The authors extend robust Markov decision processes to a model-free setting where sampling is possible but model parameters are inaccessible.

They define robust versions of Q-learning, Sarsa, and temporal-difference learning. Their convergence results establish an approximately optimal robust policy and an approximate value function, respectively. The approximation qualifications are part of the results: the aim is reliable learning under model mismatch rather than exact recovery of behavior in the true environment.

For larger problems, the authors use function approximation and prove convergence in two settings. One covers robust approximate policy and value iteration with linear architectures under mild assumptions. The other introduces a mean squared robust projected Bellman error and stochastic gradient algorithms guaranteed to reach a local minimum. These provide distinct routes for extending robust learning beyond small state spaces.
summary.tldr: Robust model-free learning algorithms provide qualified convergence guarantees when training uses an approximate environment.

title: Reinforcement Learning under Model Mismatch

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) in partially observable settings is challenging because the agent’s observations are not Markov. Recently proposed methods can learn variable-order Markov models of the underlying process but have steep memory requirements and are sensitive to aliasing between observation histories due to sensor noise. This paper proposes dynamic-depth context tree weighting (D2-CTW), a model-learning method that addresses these limitations. D2-CTW dynamically expands a suffix tree while ensuring that the size of the model, but not its depth, remains bounded. We show that D2-CTW approximately matches the performance of state-of-the-art alternatives at stochastic time-series prediction while using at least an order of magnitude less memory. We also apply D2-CTW to model-based RL, showing that, on tasks that require memory of past observations, D2-CTW can learn without prior knowledge of a good state representation, or even the length of history upon which such a representation should depend.
