paragraphs: Neural emulators learn to approximate the behavior of systems described by partial differential equations using numerical simulation data. It is tempting to assume that an emulator cannot be more accurate than the solver supplying that data. This paper identifies cases where a network trained entirely on lower-fidelity simulations performs better than its source solver against a higher-fidelity reference.

The analysis focuses on predictions rolled forward over multiple steps. It examines how the network's inductive biases, training objective, and the numerical solver's error characteristics interact. These interactions can produce learned dynamics that are more regularized or accumulate errors more favorably than the original solver's dynamics.

Experiments across different equations and standard neural architectures support this phenomenon. The result is conditional: superiority occurs within particular operating regimes, rather than following automatically from training a neural emulator. It matters for evaluation because matching the training solver and matching a more accurate physical reference are different goals. An emulator may reduce some numerical artifacts present in the data it learned from.
summary.tldr: Neural PDE emulators can outperform their training solvers in specific regimes through favorable regularization and error accumulation.

title: Neural Emulator Superiority: When Machine Learning for PDEs Surpasses its Training Data

abstract: Multi-task learning is a paradigm shown to improve the performance of related tasks through their joint learning. However, for real-world data, it is usually difficult to assess the task relatedness and joint learning with unrelated tasks may lead to serious performance degradations. To this end, we propose a framework that groups the tasks based on their relatedness in a low dimensional subspace and allows a varying degree of relatedness among tasks by sharing the subspace bases across the groups. This provides the flexibility of no sharing when two sets of tasks are unrelated and partial/total sharing when the tasks are related. Importantly, the number of task-groups and the subspace dimensionality are automatically inferred from the data. This feature keeps the model beyond a specific set of parameters. To realize our framework, we present a novel Bayesian nonparametric prior that extends the traditional hierarchical beta process prior using a Dirichlet process to permit potentially infinite number of child beta processes. We apply our model for multi-task regression and classification applications. Experimental results using several synthetic and real-world datasets show the superiority of our model to other recent state-of-the-art multi-task learning methods.

paragraphs: Learning related tasks together can improve performance, but sharing information with unrelated tasks can cause serious degradation. This paper proposes a multitask framework that learns how tasks are related instead of committing to uniform sharing. It groups tasks in a low-dimensional subspace and allows the groups themselves to share subspace bases.

That construction supports several degrees of relatedness. Unrelated groups can avoid sharing, while related groups can share some or all of their bases. The number of groups and the subspace dimensionality are inferred from data. To provide this flexibility, the authors extend a hierarchical beta process prior using a Dirichlet process, permitting potentially infinitely many child beta processes.

The model is applied to both regression and classification across multiple tasks. Experiments on several synthetic and real-world datasets report better performance than other recent state-of-the-art multitask methods. The stated advantage is a flexible representation of task relationships: the model can choose both how much structure to use and where sharing should occur.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric multitask model learns task groups, subspace size, and degrees of sharing, outperforming comparison methods in the reported experiments.

title: Factorial Multi-Task Learning : A Bayesian Nonparametric Approach

abstract: We provide a first PAC-Bayesian analysis for domain adaptation (DA) which arises when the learning and test distributions differ. It relies on a novel distribution pseudodistance based on a disagreement averaging. Using this measure, we derive a PAC-Bayesian DA bound for the stochastic Gibbs classifier. This bound has the advantage of being directly optimizable for any hypothesis space. We specialize it to linear classifiers, and design a learning algorithm which shows interesting results on a synthetic problem and on a popular sentiment annotation task. This opens the door to tackling DA tasks by making use of all the PAC-Bayesian tools.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation concerns learning when the distribution supplying training examples differs from the distribution encountered at test time. This paper develops a PAC-Bayesian analysis of that problem, connecting guarantees about prediction to a framework that reasons about distributions over classifiers. The authors present this as the first PAC-Bayesian treatment of domain adaptation.

The central construction measures differences between domains through average classifier disagreement. Rather than describing distribution differences independently of prediction, it uses how classifiers disagree to define a new pseudodistance. The authors then use this quantity to bound the performance of a stochastic Gibbs classifier. A useful feature of the bound is that it can be optimized directly for any hypothesis space.

The paper specializes the analysis to linear classifiers and derives a learning algorithm from it. Experiments on a synthetic problem and a sentiment annotation task produce results the authors describe as interesting. The contribution is therefore both a theoretical framework and a concrete algorithm, opening a route for applying further PAC-Bayesian tools to adaptation.
summary.tldr: A disagreement-based PAC-Bayesian bound provides an optimizable framework for domain adaptation and yields a concrete algorithm for linear classifiers.

title: A PAC-Bayesian Approach for Domain Adaptation with Specialization to Linear Classifiers

abstract: We consider the problem of recovering the graph structure of a “hub-networked” Ising model given iid samples, under high-dimensional settings, where number of nodes p could be potentially larger than the number of samples n. By a “hub-networked” graph, we mean a graph with a few “hub nodes” with very large degrees. State of the art estimators for Ising models have a sample complexity that scales polynomially with the maximum node-degree, and are thus ill-suited to recovering such graphs with a few hub nodes. Some recent proposals for specifically recovering hub graphical models do not come with theoretical guarantees, and even empirically provide limited improvements over vanilla Ising model estimators. Here, we show that under such low sample settings, instead of estimating “difficult” components such as hub-neighborhoods, we can use quantitative indicators of our inability to do so, and thereby identify hub-nodes. This simple procedure allows us to recover hub-networked graphs with very strong statistical guarantees even under very low sample settings.

paragraphs: This paper studies recovery of an Ising model's graph when a few nodes are connected to many others. Such hubs create a particular difficulty in high dimensions, where the number of nodes may exceed the number of independent, identically distributed samples. Existing estimators have sample requirements that grow polynomially with the largest node degree.

The authors turn the difficulty of estimating hub neighborhoods into useful information. Instead of requiring accurate estimates of these difficult components at the outset, they use quantitative indicators of the inability to estimate them. Those indicators allow the procedure to identify hub nodes even when samples are scarce.

The paper shows that this strategy supports recovery of hub-networked graphs with strong statistical guarantees in low-sample settings. The contribution is a change in how estimation difficulty is used: it becomes evidence about the graph's organization. This directly addresses the mismatch between a network containing only a few highly connected nodes and methods whose sample demands are governed by the single largest degree.
summary.tldr: Quantifying difficulty in estimating neighborhoods helps identify hubs and recover hub-networked Ising graphs from few samples.

title: Learning Graphs with a Few Hubs

abstract: Bayesian methods are ubiquitous in machine learning. Nevertheless, the analysis of empirical results is typically performed by frequentist tests. This implies dealing with null hypothesis significance tests and p-values, even though the shortcomings of such methods are well known. We propose a nonparametric Bayesian version of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test using a Dirichlet process (DP) based prior. We address in two different ways the problem of how to choose the infinite dimensional parameter that characterizes the DP. The proposed test has all the traditional strengths of the Bayesian approach; for instance, unlike the frequentist tests, it allows verifying the null hypothesis, not only rejecting it, and taking decision which minimize the expected loss. Moreover, one of the solutions proposed to model the infinitedimensional parameter of the DP, allows isolating instances in which the traditional frequentist test is guessing at random. We show results dealing with the comparison of two classifiers using real and simulated data.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Bayesian alternative to the Wilcoxon signed-rank test for comparing empirical results, including the performance of two classifiers. The motivation is that machine learning often uses Bayesian models but evaluates their results through frequentist significance tests and p-values. The proposed test brings that comparison step into a nonparametric Bayesian framework.

The method uses a Dirichlet process prior. A central modeling question is how to choose the infinite-dimensional parameter that characterizes this prior, and the authors offer two different treatments. This choice matters because the prior is part of how the test represents uncertainty and supports conclusions from the observed comparisons.

The authors describe benefits including the ability to support the null hypothesis and to choose decisions that minimize expected loss. They also report that one treatment of the prior parameter identifies instances where the conventional frequentist test behaves like random guessing. Comparisons on real and simulated classifier results illustrate the proposed approach.
summary.tldr: A Dirichlet process prior turns signed-rank comparison into a Bayesian test that can support the null hypothesis and guide decisions by expected loss.

title: A Bayesian Wilcoxon signed-rank test based on the Dirichlet process

abstract: We consider the problem of discriminative factor analysis for data that are in general non-Gaussian. A Bayesian model based on the ranks of the data is proposed. We first introduce a max-margin version of the rank-likelihood. A discriminative factor model is then developed, integrating the new max-margin rank-likelihood and (linear) Bayesian support vector machines, which are also built on the max-margin principle. The discriminative factor model is further extended to the nonlinear case through mixtures of local linear classifiers, via Dirichlet processes. Fully local conjugacy of the model yields efficient inference with both Markov Chain Monte Carlo and variational Bayes approaches. Extensive experiments on benchmark and real data demonstrate superior performance of the proposed model and its potential for applications in computational biology.

paragraphs: This paper develops discriminative factor analysis for observations that need not be Gaussian. Its Bayesian model uses the ranks of the data, making relative ordering central to the observation model. The first contribution is a max-margin version of the rank-likelihood, which brings a margin-based principle into the modeling of those ordered observations.

The authors combine that likelihood with linear Bayesian support vector machines to create a discriminative factor model. Both components use a max-margin principle, linking the treatment of observations with the classification component. They then extend the classifier to nonlinear behavior by using a Dirichlet process mixture of local linear classifiers.

The model retains local conjugacy, enabling efficient inference through either Markov chain Monte Carlo or variational Bayes. Experiments on benchmark and real data report superior performance and suggest potential applications in computational biology. The contribution brings together rank-based modeling, discriminative factors, and flexible classification while maintaining inference procedures that the authors describe as computationally efficient.
summary.tldr: A rank-based Bayesian factor model combines max-margin observation modeling with linear or nonlinear classification for non-Gaussian data.

title: Non-Gaussian Discriminative Factor Models via the Max-Margin Rank-Likelihood

abstract: We propose the group knockoff filter, a method for false discovery rate control in a linear regression setting where the features are grouped, and we would like to select a set of relevant groups which have a nonzero effect on the response. By considering the set of true and false discoveries at the group level, this method gains power relative to sparse regression methods. We also apply our method to the multitask regression problem where multiple response variables share similar sparsity patterns across the set of possible features. Empirically, the group knockoff filter successfully controls false discoveries at the group level in both settings, with substantially more discoveries made by leveraging the group structure.

We also apply our method to the multitask regression problem where multiple response variables share similar sparsity patterns across the set of possible features. paragraphs: The paper studies variable selection in linear regression when features come in groups. The goal is to identify groups with a nonzero effect on the response while controlling false discoveries. This makes a group, rather than an individual feature, the unit at which a selected result is judged relevant or irrelevant.

The authors propose the group knockoff filter for this setting. By defining discoveries at the group level and using the grouping structure, the method gains power relative to sparse regression methods. They also apply it to multitask regression, where several response variables share similar patterns of relevant features. In that setting, shared sparsity provides structure that the selection procedure can use.

Empirically, the method controls false discoveries at the group level in both grouped-feature and multitask regression. It also makes substantially more discoveries by exploiting the available group structure. These findings indicate that organizing selection around meaningful groups can improve the ability to find relevant effects while maintaining the stated group-level error control.
summary.tldr: The group knockoff filter uses grouped structure to find more relevant feature groups while empirically controlling group-level false discoveries.

title: The knockoff filter for FDR control in group-sparse and multitask regression

abstract: We address the problem of detecting distribution changes in multivariate data streams by means of histograms. Histograms are very general and flexible models, which have been relatively ignored in the change-detection literature as they often require a number of bins that grows unfeasibly with the data dimension. We present QuantTree, a recursive binary splitting scheme that adaptively defines the histogram bins to ease the detection of any distribution change. Our design scheme implies that i) we can easily control the overall number of bins and ii) the bin probabilities do not depend on the distribution of stationary data. This latter is a very relevant aspect in change detection, since thresholds of tests statistics based on these histograms (e.g., the Pearson statistic or the total variation) can be numerically computed from univariate and synthetically generated data, yet guaranteeing a controlled false positive rate. Our experiments show that the proposed histograms are very effective in detecting changes in high dimensional data streams, and that the resulting thresholds can effectively control the false positive rate, even when the number of training samples is relatively small.

paragraphs: QuantTree detects changes in the distribution of multivariate streaming data using histograms. A common difficulty with histograms is that the number of bins can become unmanageable as dimensionality increases. The paper introduces an adaptive construction based on recursive binary splitting, allowing the overall bin count to be controlled.

A key property of the construction is that bin probabilities do not depend on the particular distribution of stationary data. This makes it possible to calibrate change-detection thresholds using synthetically generated one-dimensional data. Those thresholds can then be used with histogram-based test statistics, such as Pearson’s statistic or total variation, while controlling the false positive rate.

This connects the histogram design to a practical statistical requirement: distinguishing a real distribution change from an alarm raised during unchanged behavior. Experiments show effective change detection in high-dimensional streams and effective false-positive control even with relatively few training samples. The contribution combines manageable histogram complexity with a calibration method that does not depend on the original stationary distribution.
summary.tldr: QuantTree builds adaptive histograms for detecting distribution changes with controlled bin counts and false-positive rates.

title: QuantTree: Histograms for Change Detection in Multivariate Data Streams

abstract: Bayesian optimization is known to be difficult to scale to high dimensions, because the acquisition step requires solving a non-convex optimization problem in the same search space. In order to scale the method and keep its benefits, we propose an algorithm (LineBO) that restricts the problem to a sequence of iteratively chosen one-dimensional sub-problems that can be solved efficiently. We show that our algorithm converges globally and obtains a fast local rate when the function is strongly convex. Further, if the objective has an invariant subspace, our method automatically adapts to the effective dimension without changing the algorithm. When combined with the SafeOpt algorithm to solve the sub-problems, we obtain the first safe Bayesian optimization algorithm with theoretical guarantees applicable in high-dimensional settings. We evaluate our method on multiple synthetic benchmarks, where we obtain competitive performance. Further, we deploy our algorithm to optimize the beam intensity of the Swiss Free Electron Laser with up to 40 parameters while satisfying safe operation constraints.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization becomes difficult in high dimensions partly because choosing the next evaluation requires solving a nonconvex optimization problem over the original search space. LineBO addresses this bottleneck by replacing that acquisition problem with a sequence of adaptively selected one-dimensional subproblems. Each step searches along a line while the overall procedure explores the larger space.

The authors establish global convergence and a fast local convergence rate when the function is strongly convex. They also show automatic adaptation to effective dimension when the objective has an invariant subspace. That qualification matters: the dimension-adaptation result depends on structure in the objective, rather than applying indiscriminately to every high-dimensional function.

Combining LineBO with SafeOpt for the individual subproblems produces a safe Bayesian optimization method with theoretical guarantees for high-dimensional settings. The authors report competitive performance on synthetic benchmarks and deploy the method to optimize beam intensity at the Swiss Free Electron Laser. That application uses up to 40 parameters while respecting safe operation constraints, demonstrating the approach in a physical optimization task.
summary.tldr: LineBO scales Bayesian optimization through adaptive one-dimensional searches, with convergence results and a SafeOpt-based extension for safe operation.

title: Adaptive and Safe Bayesian Optimization in High Dimensions via One-Dimensional Subspaces

abstract: Neural networks are known to be a class of highly expressive functions able to fit even random input-output mappings with 100% accuracy. In this work we present properties of neural networks that complement this aspect of expressivity. By using tools from Fourier analysis, we highlight a learning bias of deep networks towards low frequency functions – i.e. functions that vary globally without local fluctuations – which manifests itself as a frequency-dependent learning speed. Intuitively, this property is in line with the observation that over-parameterized networks prioritize learning simple patterns that generalize across data samples. We also investigate the role of the shape of the data manifold by presenting empirical and theoretical evidence that, somewhat counter-intuitively, learning higher frequencies gets easier with increasing manifold complexity.

By using tools from Fourier analysis, we highlight a learning bias of deep networks towards low frequency functions – i.e. functions that vary globally without local fluctuations – which manifests itself as a frequency-dependent learning speed. Intuitively, this property is in line with the observation that over-parameterized networks prioritize learning simple patterns that generalize across data samples. We also investigate the role of the shape of the data manifold by presenting empirical and theoretical evidence that, somewhat counter-intuitively, learning higher frequencies gets easier with increasing manifold complexity.

paragraphs: Neural networks can represent extremely complicated functions, including arbitrary labels on training examples. Expressive capacity alone, however, does not determine which patterns a network learns first. This paper studies that distinction through the frequencies of the functions learned during training.

Using Fourier analysis, the authors identify a bias toward low-frequency functions: patterns that vary broadly across the input rather than fluctuating rapidly in small regions. The bias appears as a frequency-dependent learning speed. This offers a way to understand why an overparameterized network can prioritize comparatively simple, broadly shared patterns despite having enough capacity to memorize more complicated ones.

The paper also examines the geometry of the data manifold. Its theoretical and empirical evidence indicates that higher-frequency functions can become easier to learn as manifold complexity increases. Thus the learning preference is not described solely by the network’s expressive power; it also depends on how the data occupy the input space. The abstract presents this as an explanatory property, rather than a universal generalization guarantee.
summary.tldr: Networks learn lower frequencies preferentially, while the geometry of the data manifold changes how difficult higher frequencies are.

title: On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks

abstract: Testing Bayesian Networks (TBNs) were introduced recently to represent a set of distributions, one of which is selected based on the given evidence and used for reasoning. TBNs are more expressive than classical Bayesian Networks (BNs): Marginal queries correspond to multi-linear functions in BNs and to piecewise multi-linear functions in TBNs. Moreover, TBN queries are universal approximators, like neural networks. In this paper, we study conditional independence in TBNs, showing that it can be inferred from d-separation as in BNs. We also study the role of TBN expressiveness and independence in dealing with the problem of learning with incomplete models (i.e., ones that miss nodes or edges from the data-generating model). Finally, we illustrate our results on a number of concrete examples, including a case study on Hidden Markov Models.

paragraphs: Testing Bayesian Networks represent a collection of probability distributions and select one according to the evidence supplied for a query. This gives them more expressive query behavior than ordinary Bayesian Networks. Where ordinary networks produce multilinear functions for marginal queries, testing networks produce piecewise multilinear functions. Their queries also have a universal approximation capability comparable to that of neural networks.

The paper investigates whether this additional flexibility retains a familiar way to reason about conditional independence. Conditional independence describes when learning one variable provides no further information about another once certain variables are known. The authors show that d-separation, the graphical criterion used in ordinary Bayesian Networks, can also establish conditional independence in Testing Bayesian Networks.

They further examine how expressiveness and independence matter when learning with an incomplete model, meaning a model whose structure omits nodes or edges present in the process generating the data. Concrete examples, including a Hidden Markov Model case study, illustrate the results. The contribution connects flexible probabilistic modeling with graphical reasoning that remains useful for understanding which dependencies a model represents.
summary.tldr: Testing Bayesian Networks retain d-separation-based independence reasoning while supporting more expressive probabilistic queries.

title: Conditional Independence in Testing Bayesian Networks

abstract: The problem of market clearing is to set a price for an item such that quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. In this work, we cast the problem of predicting clearing prices into a learning framework and use the resulting models to perform revenue optimization in auctions and markets with contextual information. The economic intuition behind market clearing allows us to obtain fine-grained control over the aggressiveness of the resulting pricing policy, grounded in theory. To evaluate our approach, we fit a model of clearing prices over a massive dataset of bids in display ad auctions from a major ad exchange. The learned prices outperform other modeling techniques in the literature in terms of revenue and efficiency trade-offs. Because of the convex nature of the clearing loss function, the convergence rate of our method is as fast as linear regression.

paragraphs: A market-clearing price balances the quantity buyers demand with the quantity sellers supply. This paper turns prediction of that price into a learning problem, then uses the learned models for revenue optimization in auctions and markets with contextual information. The economic target provides a structured basis for learning a pricing policy from data.

The authors use the intuition behind market clearing to obtain theoretically grounded control over how aggressive the pricing policy is. This matters because pricing is evaluated through both revenue and efficiency, so the desired behavior involves a trade-off. Their clearing loss is convex, and they state that the method’s convergence rate is as fast as that of linear regression.

For evaluation, they fit clearing-price models to a large collection of display-ad auction bids from a major ad exchange. The learned prices outperform other modeling techniques from the literature in the reported revenue–efficiency trade-offs. The evidence therefore connects the learning formulation to an operational pricing setting, while the convex objective supports efficient optimization and explicit control over policy behavior.
summary.tldr: Learning market-clearing prices yields convex optimization and controllable pricing policies with improved auction revenue–efficiency trade-offs in the evaluation.

title: Learning to Clear the Market

abstract: This paper presents a methodology and numerical algorithms for constructing accelerated gradient flows on the space of probability distributions. In particular, we extend the recent variational formulation of accelerated methods in (Wibisono et al., 2016) from vector valued variables to probability distributions. The variational problem is modeled as a mean-field optimal control problem. A quantitative estimate on the asymptotic convergence rate is provided based on a Lyapunov function construction, when the objective functional is displacement convex. An important special case is considered where the objective functional is the relative entropy. For this case, two numerical approximations are presented to implement the Hamilton’s equations as a system of N interacting particles. The algorithm is numerically illustrated and compared with the MCMC and Hamiltonian MCMC algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to accelerate optimization when the object being updated is an entire probability distribution. It extends a variational formulation of accelerated optimization from vector variables to distributions. This shifts the question from how a point should move through a parameter space to how a distribution should evolve toward an objective.

The authors formulate this evolution as a mean-field optimal control problem. They construct a Lyapunov function to obtain a quantitative estimate of the asymptotic convergence rate. That result depends on the objective being displacement convex, so the stated theoretical guarantee concerns a particular class of objectives rather than arbitrary optimization over distributions.

For the important case where the objective is relative entropy, the paper provides two numerical approximations. These implement Hamilton’s equations through a collection of interacting particles, connecting the distribution-level formulation to computable algorithms. Numerical illustrations compare the resulting algorithm with MCMC and Hamiltonian MCMC. The abstract reports these comparisons without claiming a particular performance advantage over either method.
summary.tldr: The paper develops accelerated optimization flows for probability distributions, with conditional convergence analysis and interacting-particle implementations.

title: Accelerated Flow for Probability Distributions

abstract: For text analysis, one often resorts to a lossy representation that either completely ignores word order or embeds each word as a low-dimensional dense feature vector. In this paper, we propose convolutional Poisson factor analysis (CPFA) that directly operates on a lossless representation that processes the words in each document as a sequence of high-dimensional one-hot vectors. To boost its performance, we further propose the convolutional Poisson gamma belief network (CPGBN) that couples CPFA with the gamma belief network via a novel probabilistic pooling layer. CPFA forms words into phrases and captures very specific phrase-level topics, and CPGBN further builds a hierarchy of increasingly more general phrase-level topics. For efficient inference, we develop both a Gibbs sampler and a Weibull distribution based convolutional variational auto-encoder. Experimental results demonstrate that CPGBN can extract high-quality text latent representations that capture the word order information, and hence can be leveraged as a building block to enrich a wide variety of existing latent variable models that ignore word order.

paragraphs: This paper develops a probabilistic text model that keeps word identity and word order in its input representation. It represents each document as a sequence of high-dimensional one-hot vectors, rather than discarding order or first compressing words into dense vectors. Convolutional Poisson factor analysis, or CPFA, operates directly on this sequence.

CPFA groups words into phrases and discovers specific topics at the phrase level. The authors extend it into a convolutional Poisson gamma belief network by connecting CPFA to a gamma belief network through a new probabilistic pooling layer. This produces a hierarchy in which more specific phrase topics feed into increasingly general topics.

The paper develops two inference approaches: a Gibbs sampler and a convolutional variational autoencoder based on Weibull distributions. Experiments show that the resulting model learns high-quality latent text representations that capture word order. The stated broader opportunity is to use this component to enrich existing latent-variable models that otherwise ignore order, bringing phrase structure into their representations.
summary.tldr: A convolutional probabilistic text model preserves word order while learning a hierarchy of phrase-level topics.

title: Convolutional Poisson Gamma Belief Network

abstract: The standard risk minimization paradigm of machine learning is brittle when operating in environments whose test distributions are different from the training distribution due to spurious correlations. Training on data from many environments and finding invariant predictors reduces the effect of spurious features by concentrating models on features that have a causal relationship with the outcome. In this work, we pose such invariant risk minimization as finding the Nash equilibrium of an ensemble game among several environments. By doing so, we develop a simple training algorithm that uses best response dynamics and, in our experiments, yields similar or better empirical accuracy with much lower variance than the challenging bi-level optimization problem of Arjovsky et al. (2019). One key theoretical contribution is showing that the set of Nash equilibria for the proposed game are equivalent to the set of invariant predictors for any finite number of environments, even with nonlinear classifiers and transformations. As a result, our method also retains the generalization guarantees to a large set of environments shown in Arjovsky et al. (2019). The proposed algorithm adds to the collection of successful game-theoretic machine learning algorithms such as generative adversarial networks.

paragraphs: Predictors can fail when correlations learned during training change in a new environment. Invariant risk minimization uses multiple training environments to seek predictors that remain valid across them, reducing reliance on spurious features. This paper reformulates that search as an ensemble game played among the environments.

The key theoretical result equates the game's Nash equilibria with invariant predictors for any finite number of environments. The equivalence includes nonlinear classifiers and transformations. A Nash equilibrium describes a configuration where no player benefits from changing its own strategy alone; here, that equilibrium condition provides a game-theoretic characterization of the desired predictors.

The reformulation leads to a simple training algorithm based on best-response dynamics. In the reported experiments, it achieves similar or better accuracy with substantially lower variance than the earlier bilevel optimization approach. The method also retains the earlier framework's generalization guarantees over a large set of environments. The paper thus connects a theoretical equivalence to a training procedure with favorable empirical behavior.
summary.tldr: Casting invariant prediction as a game yields an equilibrium characterization and a simple training algorithm with lower empirical variance.

title: Invariant Risk Minimization Games

abstract: Meta-learning algorithms produce feature extractors which achieve state-of-the-art performance on few-shot classification. While the literature is rich with meta-learning methods, little is known about why the resulting feature extractors perform so well. We develop a better understanding of the underlying mechanics of meta-learning and the difference between models trained using meta-learning and models which are trained classically. In doing so, we introduce and verify several hypotheses for why meta-learned models perform better. Furthermore, we develop a regularizer which boosts the performance of standard training routines for few-shot classification. In many cases, our routine outperforms meta-learning while simultaneously running an order of magnitude faster.

paragraphs: Few-shot classification requires useful predictions from very few examples of a task. Meta-learning produces feature extractors that perform strongly in this setting, but the reasons for their success are not well understood. This paper investigates what distinguishes those learned representations from representations produced by conventional training.

The authors introduce and verify several hypotheses about why meta-learned models perform better. They then use that investigation to develop a regularizer that improves ordinary training routines for few-shot classification. The contribution therefore connects an explanatory study of feature representations with a concrete modification to how standard models are trained.

In many cases, the resulting routine outperforms meta-learning while running an order of magnitude faster. The qualification matters: the reported advantage holds in many evaluated cases, rather than being a universal ranking of training methods. The finding suggests that understanding the properties of effective representations can make some benefits of meta-learning accessible through a faster conventional training procedure.
summary.tldr: Studying meta-learned features yields a regularizer that improves standard few-shot training and often beats meta-learning while running substantially faster.

title: Unraveling Meta-Learning: Understanding Feature Representations for Few-Shot Tasks

abstract: Performance evaluations are critical for quantifying algorithmic advances in reinforcement learning. Recent reproducibility analyses have shown that reported performance results are often inconsistent and difficult to replicate. In this work, we argue that the inconsistency of performance stems from the use of flawed evaluation metrics. Taking a step towards ensuring that reported results are consistent, we propose a new comprehensive evaluation methodology for reinforcement learning algorithms that produces reliable measurements of performance both on a single environment and when aggregated across environments. We demonstrate this method by evaluating a broad class of reinforcement learning algorithms on standard benchmark tasks.

We demonstrate this method by evaluating a broad class of reinforcement learning algorithms on standard benchmark tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning progress is often assessed by comparing reported algorithm performance. Those comparisons become difficult to trust when results are inconsistent or hard to reproduce. This paper examines evaluation itself, arguing that flawed performance metrics are a source of the inconsistency identified by reproducibility analyses.

The authors propose a comprehensive evaluation methodology intended to produce reliable measurements at two levels. One level concerns an algorithm's performance within a single environment. The other concerns how performance is combined across environments. Addressing both matters because an overall comparison depends on the individual measurements as well as the procedure used to aggregate them.

The methodology is demonstrated by evaluating a broad class of reinforcement learning algorithms on standard benchmark tasks. Its contribution is therefore a way to assess algorithmic advances, rather than a new learning rule. The stated findings support treating measurement design as part of reproducible research: the evaluation procedure should make both individual-task results and cross-task comparisons reliable.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes a reinforcement learning evaluation methodology for reliable performance measurement within and across environments.

title: Evaluating the Performance of Reinforcement Learning Algorithms

abstract: In visual planning (VP), an agent learns to plan goal-directed behavior from observations of a dynamical system obtained offline, e.g., images obtained from self-supervised robot interaction. Most previous works on VP approached the problem by planning in a learned latent space, resulting in low-quality visual plans, and difficult training algorithms. Here, instead, we propose a simple VP method that plans directly in image space and displays competitive performance. We build on the semi-parametric topological memory (SPTM) method: image samples are treated as nodes in a graph, the graph connectivity is learned from image sequence data, and planning can be performed using conventional graph search methods. We propose two modifications on SPTM. First, we train an energy-based graph connectivity function using contrastive predictive coding that admits stable training. Second, to allow zero-shot planning in new domains, we learn a conditional VAE model that generates images given a context describing the domain, and use these hallucinated samples for building the connectivity graph and planning. We show that this simple approach significantly outperform the SOTA VP methods, in terms of both plan interpretability and success rate when using the plan to guide a trajectory-following controller. Interestingly, our method can pick up non-trivial visual properties of objects, such as their geometry, and account for it in the plans.

paragraphs: Visual planning learns goal-directed behavior from previously collected observations, such as images of robot interactions. This paper plans directly with images by organizing them into a graph: images become nodes, learned connections describe possible transitions, and conventional graph search produces a plan. This gives the planned route an explicit visual form.

The method extends semi-parametric topological memory in two ways. First, an energy-based connectivity function is trained using contrastive predictive coding, providing stable training. Second, a conditional variational autoencoder generates images from a description of the domain. These generated images supply graph nodes, allowing the system to construct plans in new domains without prior interaction there.

The authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art visual planning methods in plan interpretability and in success when a trajectory-following controller executes the plan. They also find that the method can account for nontrivial object properties, including geometry. The results connect image generation to planning through a searchable graph, while keeping the intermediate plan visually inspectable.
summary.tldr: Generated domain-conditioned images form a searchable planning graph that improves visual interpretability and controller success in new domains.

title: Hallucinative Topological Memory for Zero-Shot Visual Planning

abstract: We present a strikingly simple proof that two rules are sufficient to automate gradient descent: 1) don’t increase the stepsize too fast and 2) don’t overstep the local curvature. No need for functional values, no line search, no information about the function except for the gradients. By following these rules, you get a method adaptive to the local geometry, with convergence guarantees depending only on the smoothness in a neighborhood of a solution. Given that the problem is convex, our method converges even if the global smoothness constant is infinity. As an illustration, it can minimize arbitrary continuously twice-differentiable convex function. We examine its performance on a range of convex and nonconvex problems, including logistic regression and matrix factorization.

paragraphs: Gradient descent needs a step size that determines how far each update moves. This paper gives two sufficient rules for automating that choice: limit how quickly the step size grows, and keep it compatible with local curvature. Together, these rules produce an algorithm that adjusts to the geometry encountered during optimization.

The procedure uses gradients without requiring function values or a line search. Its convergence guarantees depend on smoothness near a solution, rather than a finite smoothness bound over the entire problem. For convex problems, the method can therefore converge even when the global smoothness constant is infinite. The authors illustrate this reach with continuously twice-differentiable convex functions.

The paper also examines performance on convex and nonconvex problems, including logistic regression and matrix factorization. Those evaluations broaden the practical investigation, while the stated convergence claim retains its convexity qualification. The central result is that these two step-size rules are sufficient to obtain locally adaptive behavior with convergence guarantees that do not demand global smoothness.
summary.tldr: Two gradient-based step-size rules yield an adaptive method with convex convergence guarantees depending on smoothness near a solution.

title: Adaptive Gradient Descent without Descent

abstract: Adversarial examples are malicious inputs crafted to induce misclassification. Commonly studied \emph{sensitivity-based} adversarial examples introduce semantically-small changes to an input that result in a different model prediction. This paper studies a complementary failure mode, \emph{invariance-based} adversarial examples, that introduce minimal semantic changes that modify an input’s true label yet preserve the model’s prediction. We demonstrate fundamental tradeoffs between these two types of adversarial examples. We show that defenses against sensitivity-based attacks actively harm a model’s accuracy on invariance-based attacks, and that new approaches are needed to resist both attack types. In particular, we break state-of-the-art adversarially-trained and \emph{certifiably-robust} models by generating small perturbations that the models are (provably) robust to, yet that change an input’s class according to human labelers. Finally, we formally show that the existence of excessively invariant classifiers arises from the presence of \emph{overly-robust} predictive features in standard datasets.

This paper studies a complementary failure mode, \emph{invariance-based} adversarial examples, that introduce minimal semantic changes that modify an input’s true label yet preserve the model’s prediction. We demonstrate fundamental tradeoffs between these two types of adversarial examples. We show that defenses against sensitivity-based attacks actively harm a model’s accuracy on invariance-based attacks, and that new approaches are needed to resist both attack types. In particular, we break state-of-the-art adversarially-trained and \emph{certifiably-robust} models by generating small perturbations that the models are (provably) robust to, yet that change an input’s class according to human labelers. paragraphs: Adversarial robustness is often framed as keeping a prediction unchanged when an input changes slightly without changing its meaning. This paper examines the complementary failure: a small semantic change alters the correct label, but the model keeps its original prediction. In that case, the model is too invariant.

The authors demonstrate tradeoffs between these failure modes. Defenses targeting sensitivity-based attacks harm accuracy on invariance-based attacks in their investigation. They construct perturbations that adversarially trained and certifiably robust models resist, even though human labelers judge that the input’s class has changed. The prediction stability being protected is therefore itself responsible for an error.

Its findings show why resisting input changes is insufficient as a complete account of robustness: a useful classifier also needs to respond when the relevant meaning changes. The authors argue that new approaches are needed to address both kinds of adversarial examples.
summary.tldr: Defending against prediction changes can create excessive invariance, leaving models wrong when small input changes genuinely alter the correct class.

title: Fundamental Tradeoffs between Invariance and Sensitivity to Adversarial Perturbations

abstract: Network quantization is essential for deploying deep models to IoT devices due to its high efficiency. Most existing quantization approaches rely on the full training datasets and the time-consuming fine-tuning to retain accuracy. Post-training quantization does not have these problems, however, it has mainly been shown effective for 8-bit quantization due to the simple optimization strategy. In this paper, we propose a Bit-Split and Stitching framework (Bit-split) for lower-bit post-training quantization with minimal accuracy degradation. The proposed framework is validated on a variety of computer vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, instance segmentation, with various network architectures. Specifically, Bit-split can achieve near-original model performance even when quantizing FP32 models to INT3 without fine-tuning.

Post-training quantization avoids those requirements, but the paper describes existing simple optimization strategies as having mainly demonstrated effectiveness at eight-bit precision.

The authors propose Bit-Split and Stitching, a framework for pushing post-training quantization to lower bit widths with little accuracy loss. Its purpose is to make more aggressive numerical compression practical without fine-tuning the model. This addresses the tension between efficient deployment and preserving the behavior of the original, higher-precision network.

The framework is evaluated across image classification, object detection, and instance segmentation using various network architectures. The authors report that it can retain near-original performance even when converting 32-bit floating-point models to three-bit integer representations without fine-tuning. That finding establishes a demonstrated possibility across the evaluated work, rather than a guarantee that every model will retain its accuracy at three bits.
summary.tldr: Bit-Split and Stitching enables low-bit post-training quantization, with near-original performance demonstrated even at three bits without fine-tuning.

title: Towards Accurate Post-training Network Quantization via Bit-Split and Stitching

abstract: During the past five years the Bayesian deep learning community has developed increasingly accurate and efficient approximate inference procedures that allow for Bayesian inference in deep neural networks. However, despite this algorithmic progress and the promise of improved uncertainty quantification and sample efficiency there are—as of early 2020—no publicized deployments of Bayesian neural networks in industrial practice. In this work we cast doubt on the current understanding of Bayes posteriors in popular deep neural networks: we demonstrate through careful MCMC sampling that the posterior predictive induced by the Bayes posterior yields systematically worse predictions when compared to simpler methods including point estimates obtained from SGD. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive performance is improved significantly through the use of a “cold posterior” that overcounts evidence. Such cold posteriors sharply deviate from the Bayesian paradigm but are commonly used as heuristic in Bayesian deep learning papers. We put forward several hypotheses that could explain cold posteriors and evaluate the hypotheses through experiments. Our work questions the goal of accurate posterior approximations in Bayesian deep learning: If the true Bayes posterior is poor, what is the use of more accurate approximations? Instead, we argue that it is timely to focus on understanding the origin of cold posteriors.

paragraphs: Bayesian deep learning often aims to approximate a neural network's posterior distribution more accurately. This paper questions whether that posterior necessarily gives the best predictive target in the popular networks studied. The authors use careful Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling to investigate predictive performance, rather than assuming that more faithful posterior approximation will improve predictions.

Their experiments find that predictions induced by the Bayes posterior are systematically worse than those from simpler methods, including point estimates learned with stochastic gradient descent. They also find substantial improvements from a cold posterior, which gives the observed evidence more weight than standard Bayesian updating does.

The authors propose several possible explanations for this cold-posterior effect and evaluate them experimentally. Their argument is that understanding why modified posteriors predict better deserves attention alongside improving inference algorithms. The findings challenge the predictive value of the standard posterior in the investigated settings; they do not establish that Bayesian inference is universally inferior. The central issue is whether the distribution being approximated is itself an effective predictive choice.
summary.tldr: Careful sampling finds poorer predictions from standard Bayes posteriors in the studied neural networks and substantial gains from cold posteriors.

title: How Good is the Bayes Posterior in Deep Neural Networks Really?

abstract: We study fast algorithms for computing basic properties of an n x n positive semidefinite kernel matrix K corresponding to n points x_1,...,x_n in R^d. In particular, we consider the estimating the sum of kernel matrix entries, along with its top eigenvalue and eigenvector. These are some of the most basic problems defined over kernel matrices. We show that the sum of matrix entries can be estimated up to a multiplicative factor of 1+\epsilon in time sublinear in n and linear in d for many popular kernel functions, including the Gaussian, exponential, and rational quadratic kernels. For these kernels, we also show that the top eigenvalue (and a witnessing approximate eigenvector) can be approximated to a multiplicative factor of 1+\epsilon in time sub-quadratic in n and linear in d. Our algorithms represent significant advances in the best known runtimes for these problems. They leverage the positive definiteness of the kernel matrix, along with a recent line of work on efficient kernel density estimation.

paragraphs: A kernel matrix records pairwise kernel values among a collection of points. This paper studies how to approximate basic properties of a positive semidefinite kernel matrix without paying the full cost of handling all its entries. The targets are the sum of entries, the largest eigenvalue, and an associated approximate eigenvector.

For several popular kernels, including Gaussian, exponential, and rational quadratic kernels, the authors estimate the entry sum within a multiplicative factor of 1 + epsilon in time sublinear in the number of points and linear in their dimension. They also approximate the largest eigenvalue within that factor, with a witnessing approximate eigenvector, in subquadratic time and linear dimensional dependence.

The algorithms combine positive semidefiniteness with techniques from efficient kernel density estimation. That connection allows a statistical estimation tool to support matrix computations. The stated advances concern approximation of these selected matrix properties for the covered kernels, demonstrating that useful global information can be obtained considerably faster than constructing and processing every pairwise interaction.
summary.tldr: Kernel density estimation enables faster approximations of kernel-matrix entry sums and leading eigenpairs for several widely used kernels.

title: Faster Kernel Matrix Algebra via Density Estimation

abstract: In the stochastic submodular cover problem, the goal is to select a subset of stochastic items of minimum expected cost to cover a submodular function. Solutions in this setting correspond to a sequential decision process that selects items one by one “adaptively” (depending on prior observations). While such adaptive solutions achieve the best objective, the inherently sequential nature makes them undesirable in many applications. We ask: \emph{how well can solutions with only a few adaptive rounds approximate fully-adaptive solutions?} We consider both cases where the stochastic items are independent, and where they are correlated. For both situations, we obtain nearly tight answers, establishing smooth tradeoffs between the number of adaptive rounds and the solution quality, relative to fully adaptive solutions. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets validate the practical performance of our algorithms, showing qualitative improvements in the solutions as we allow more rounds of adaptivity; in practice, solutions using just a few rounds of adaptivity are nearly as good as fully adaptive solutions.

paragraphs: Stochastic submodular cover asks how to choose uncertain items so that a coverage objective is met at minimum expected cost. A fully adaptive solution chooses items one at a time, using each observation to guide the next choice. This can achieve the best objective value, but the required sequence of decisions is undesirable in many applications.

The paper asks how much solution quality is lost when decisions are restricted to only a few adaptive rounds. It studies both independent items and correlated items. For each setting, the authors establish nearly tight tradeoffs between the number of rounds and quality relative to fully adaptive solutions, quantifying the value of additional opportunities to respond to observations.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the algorithms’ practical performance. More adaptive rounds improve solution quality, and only a few rounds produce results close to fully adaptive solutions in the reported experiments. The contribution links theoretical approximation tradeoffs to practical evidence that much of adaptivity’s value can sometimes be retained with substantially fewer sequential stages.
summary.tldr: Nearly tight bounds quantify the value of adaptive rounds in stochastic submodular cover, with a few rounds performing close to full adaptivity in experiments.

title: The Power of Adaptivity for Stochastic Submodular Cover

abstract: Sketch drawings capture the salient information of visual concepts. Previous work has shown that neural networks are capable of producing sketches of natural objects drawn from a small number of classes. While earlier approaches focus on generation quality or retrieval, we explore properties of image representations learned by training a model to produce sketches of images. We show that this generative, class-agnostic model produces informative embeddings of images from novel examples, classes, and even novel datasets in a few-shot setting. Additionally, we find that these learned representations exhibit interesting structure and compositionality.

Additionally, we find that these learned representations exhibit interesting structure and compositionality.

paragraphs: A sketch preserves selected information about a visual concept, making drawing a possible source of supervision for learning image representations. SketchEmbedNet explores this idea by training a model to produce sketches from images. The paper focuses on what the model learns internally through that task and whether those representations remain useful beyond familiar examples.

The resulting model is generative and class-agnostic. The authors examine its image embeddings, which represent images in a form usable for further learning. They show that these embeddings carry useful information in few-shot settings involving new examples, new classes, and even new datasets. This tests transfer beyond the limited sets of object classes emphasized in earlier sketch-generation work.

The learned representations also display structure and compositionality, suggesting that the drawing task captures relationships within visual concepts. The stated contribution is the usefulness of sketch-producing training for representation learning. Its findings broaden the role of drawing models beyond generation quality and retrieval by showing that imitating sketches can yield transferable information for learning unfamiliar visual concepts from few examples.
summary.tldr: Training a class-agnostic model to sketch images produces informative representations that transfer to new examples, classes, and datasets in few-shot settings.

title: SketchEmbedNet: Learning Novel Concepts by Imitating Drawings

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a two-level attention schema, Poolingformer, for long document modeling. Its first level uses a smaller sliding window pattern to aggregate information from neighbors. Its second level employs a larger window to increase receptive fields with pooling attention to reduce both computational cost and memory consumption. We first evaluate Poolingformer on two long sequence QA tasks: the monolingual NQ and the multilingual TyDi QA. Experimental results show that Poolingformer sits atop three official leaderboards measured by F1, outperforming previous state-of-the-art models by 1.9 points (79.8 vs. 77.9) on NQ long answer, 1.9 points (79.5 vs. 77.6) on TyDi QA passage answer, and 1.6 points (67.6 vs. 66.0) on TyDi QA minimal answer. We further evaluate Poolingformer on a long sequence summarization task. Experimental results on the arXiv benchmark continue to demonstrate its superior performance.

paragraphs: Poolingformer addresses long-document modeling through two levels of attention. The first level gathers information from nearby positions using a small sliding window. The second reaches across a larger window, expanding the context available to the model. Pooling attention in that larger window reduces the associated computation and memory requirements.

The design gives nearby information and wider context distinct roles within the same attention scheme. Local aggregation supplies information from neighbors, while the larger window expands the receptive field without retaining the full cost of attention across that window. The paper evaluates whether this combination translates into stronger performance on tasks involving long inputs.

On the reported official question-answering leaderboards, Poolingformer leads on NQ long answers and both TyDi QA passage and minimal answers. The reported F1 improvements over previous leading models are 1.9, 1.9, and 1.6 points, respectively. Experiments on arXiv summarization also report superior performance, extending the evidence from finding answers in long documents to producing summaries of them.
summary.tldr: Poolingformer combines local attention with pooled attention over a larger window to model long documents efficiently and improve reported task performance.

title: Poolingformer: Long Document Modeling with Pooling Attention

abstract: The deadly triad refers to the instability of a reinforcement learning algorithm when it employs off-policy learning, function approximation, and bootstrapping simultaneously. In this paper, we investigate the target network as a tool for breaking the deadly triad, providing theoretical support for the conventional wisdom that a target network stabilizes training. We first propose and analyze a novel target network update rule which augments the commonly used Polyak-averaging style update with two projections. We then apply the target network and ridge regularization in several divergent algorithms and show their convergence to regularized TD fixed points. Those algorithms are off-policy with linear function approximation and bootstrapping, spanning both policy evaluation and control, as well as both discounted and average-reward settings. In particular, we provide the first convergent linear $Q$-learning algorithms under nonrestrictive and changing behavior policies without bi-level optimization.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can become unstable when it combines data from another policy, an approximate value function, and updates that rely on existing value estimates. This combination is called the deadly triad. The paper investigates whether target networks can provide a theoretically justified way to stabilize algorithms with all three ingredients.

The authors propose a target-network update that adds two projections to the commonly used Polyak-averaging update. They combine this mechanism with ridge regularization and apply it to several algorithms that otherwise diverge. Their analysis shows convergence to regularized temporal-difference fixed points, specifying what the stabilized learning process approaches.

The results cover linear function approximation across policy evaluation and control, including both discounted and average-reward objectives. A highlighted contribution is convergent linear Q-learning under nonrestrictive, changing behavior policies, without requiring bi-level optimization. The significance is theoretical support for a particular target-network construction combined with regularization; the stated results concern these analyzed algorithms and their regularized fixed points.
summary.tldr: A modified target-network update combined with ridge regularization makes several linear reinforcement-learning algorithms converge despite the deadly triad.

title: Breaking the Deadly Triad with a Target Network

abstract: Online matching with diversity and fairness pursuit, a common building block in the recommendation and advertising, can be modeled as constrained convex programming with high entropy. While most existing approaches are based on the “single slot” assumption (i.e., assigning one item per iteration), they cannot be directly applied to cases with multiple slots, e.g., stock-aware top-N recommendation and advertising at multiple places. Particularly, the gradient computation and resource allocation are both challenging under this setting due to the absence of a closed-form solution. To overcome these obstacles, we develop a novel algorithm named Online subGradient descent for Multi-slots Allocation (OG-MA). It uses an efficient pooling algorithm to compute closed-form of the gradient then performs a roulette swapping for allocation, yielding a sub-linear regret with linear cost per iteration. Extensive experiments on synthetic and industrial data sets demonstrate that OG-MA is a fast and promising method for multi-slots online matching.

paragraphs: Recommendation and advertising systems may need to assign several items at each step while respecting resource constraints and pursuing diversity or fairness. The paper studies this as an online matching problem formulated through constrained convex programming with high entropy. Existing approaches based on assigning a single item per iteration do not directly handle the multiple-slot setting.

The proposed OG-MA algorithm addresses these two obstacles separately. An efficient pooling procedure obtains a closed-form gradient, and a roulette-swapping procedure performs the allocation. Together, these components make the online update and assignment process computationally manageable.

The analysis establishes sublinear regret with linear cost per iteration. Sublinear regret means that the accumulated shortfall measured by regret grows more slowly than the number of rounds, so its average per round decreases. Experiments on synthetic and industrial datasets support the method’s speed and promise for multiple-slot matching. The contribution combines a theoretical performance guarantee with a practical allocation mechanism for the setting studied.
summary.tldr: OG-MA handles multiple-slot online matching with efficient gradient computation and allocation, achieving sublinear regret and linear per-iteration cost.

title: Multi-slots Online Matching with High Entropy

abstract: We study covariate shift in the context of nonparametric regression. We introduce a new measure of distribution mismatch between the source and target distributions using the integrated ratio of probabilities of balls at a given radius. We use the scaling of this measure with respect to the radius to characterize the minimax rate of estimation over a family of H{ö}lder continuous functions under covariate shift. In comparison to the recently proposed notion of transfer exponent, this measure leads to a sharper rate of convergence and is more fine-grained. We accompany our theory with concrete instances of covariate shift that illustrate this sharp difference.

We introduce a new measure of distribution mismatch between the source and target distributions using the integrated ratio of probabilities of balls at a given radius. We use the scaling of this measure with respect to the radius to characterize the minimax rate of estimation over a family of H{ö}lder continuous functions under covariate shift. In comparison to the recently proposed notion of transfer exponent, this measure leads to a sharper rate of convergence and is more fine-grained. We accompany our theory with concrete instances of covariate shift that illustrate this sharp difference.

paragraphs: Covariate shift makes regression harder when the input distribution used for training differs from the distribution where predictions will be evaluated. This paper studies how that mismatch affects nonparametric regression, where the target function is described through a smoothness class rather than a fixed finite parameterization. Its central question is how to measure distribution mismatch in a way that captures estimation difficulty.

The proposed measure compares the probabilities that the source and target distributions assign to local neighborhoods, represented by balls of a chosen radius. It integrates these probability ratios and examines how the result changes as the radius varies. This connects distribution mismatch to the scale at which a regression method needs information.

For a family of Hölder-continuous functions, the authors use that scaling behavior to characterize the minimax estimation rate. They obtain a sharper, more detailed characterization than the transfer exponent provides. Concrete examples illustrate where the distinction matters, showing that different descriptions of distribution shift can lead to meaningfully different assessments of achievable estimation accuracy.
summary.tldr: A neighborhood-based measure of source–target mismatch yields sharper theoretical regression rates under covariate shift.

title: A new similarity measure for covariate shift with applications to nonparametric regression

abstract: An intriguing phenomenon that arises from the high-dimensional learning dynamics of neural networks is the phenomenon of “double descent”. The more commonly studied aspect of this phenomenon corresponds to model-wise double descent where the test error exhibits a second descent with increasing model complexity, beyond the classical U-shaped error curve. In this work, we investigate the origins of the less studied epoch-wise double descent in which the test error undergoes two non-monotonous transitions, or descents as the training time increases. We study a linear teacher-student setup exhibiting epoch-wise double descent similar to that in deep neural networks. In this setting, we derive closed-form analytical expressions describing the generalization error in terms of low-dimensional scalar macroscopic variables. We find that double descent can be attributed to distinct features being learned at different scales: as fast-learning features overfit, slower-learning features start to fit, resulting in a second descent in test error. We validate our findings through numerical simulations where our theory accurately predicts empirical findings and remains consistent with observations in deep neural networks.

paragraphs: Test error can improve, worsen, and improve again as training continues. This epoch-wise double descent differs from the better-known version associated with increasing model size. The paper investigates a mechanism behind the training-time phenomenon by studying a linear teacher-student setup that exhibits behavior resembling what is observed in deep neural networks.

Their analysis links the two descents to features being learned on different timescales. Fast-learning features begin to overfit, increasing test error, while slower-learning features subsequently become useful and drive a second decrease.

The finding makes the timing of feature acquisition central to understanding the shape of the test-error curve. Its formal derivation belongs to the linear teacher-student setting; the connection to deep networks is supported by qualitative consistency rather than an asserted universal characterization of their dynamics.
summary.tldr: A linear teacher-student analysis explains epoch-wise double descent through features learned and overfit at different timescales.

title: Multi-scale Feature Learning Dynamics: Insights for Double Descent

abstract: Domain generalization aims to improve the generalization capability of machine learning systems to out-of-distribution (OOD) data. Existing domain generalization techniques embark upon stationary and discrete environments to tackle the generalization issue caused by OOD data. However, many real-world tasks in non-stationary environments (e.g., self-driven car system, sensor measures) involve more complex and continuously evolving domain drift, which raises new challenges for the problem of domain generalization. In this paper, we formulate the aforementioned setting as the problem of evolving domain generalization. Specifically, we propose to introduce a probabilistic framework called Latent Structure-aware Sequential Autoencoder (LSSAE) to tackle the problem of evolving domain generalization via exploring the underlying continuous structure in the latent space of deep neural networks, where we aim to identify two major factors namely covariate shift and concept shift accounting for distribution shift in non-stationary environments. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that LSSAE can lead to superior performances based on the evolving domain generalization setting.

paragraphs: Domain generalization concerns performance on data distributions different from those used for training. This paper focuses on a setting where the domains themselves change continuously over time. Treating environments as stationary, separate categories can miss that progression, which motivates the authors’ formulation of evolving domain generalization.

Their method, the Latent Structure-aware Sequential Autoencoder, is a probabilistic framework that explores continuous structure in a neural network’s latent space. The contribution combines a problem formulation with a model designed around continuous change. Its stated results support paying attention to the structure of domain evolution, rather than assuming that the generalization challenge is fully captured by a collection of fixed training environments.
summary.tldr: LSSAE models continuous latent structure and two sources of distribution shift to improve generalization in evolving environments.

title: Generalizing to Evolving Domains with Latent Structure-Aware Sequential Autoencoder

abstract: Tensor decomposition is a fundamental framework to analyze data that can be represented by multi-dimensional arrays. In practice, tensor data are often accompanied with temporal information, namely the time points when the entry values were generated. This information implies abundant, complex temporal variation patterns. However, current methods always assume the factor representations of the entities in each tensor mode are static, and never consider their temporal evolution. To fill this gap, we propose NONparametric FActor Trajectory learning for dynamic tensor decomposition (NONFAT). We place Gaussian process (GP) priors in the frequency domain and conduct inverse Fourier transform via Gauss-Laguerre quadrature to sample the trajectory functions. In this way, we can overcome data sparsity and obtain robust trajectory estimates across long time horizons. Given the trajectory values at specific time points, we use a second-level GP to sample the entry values and to capture the temporal relationship between the entities. For efficient and scalable inference, we leverage the matrix Gaussian structure in the model, introduce a matrix Gaussian posterior, and develop a nested sparse variational learning algorithm. We have shown the advantage of our method in several real-world applications.

This paper addresses the mismatch between such temporal variation and methods that keep entity factors fixed throughout the observed period.

It places Gaussian-process priors in the frequency domain and constructs time-dependent functions through an inverse Fourier transform evaluated using Gauss-Laguerre quadrature. The authors use this construction to obtain robust trajectory estimates despite sparse observations and long time horizons. A second Gaussian process maps the trajectory values at particular times to tensor entries, capturing temporal relationships among entities.

The model's matrix Gaussian structure supports an inference procedure built around a matrix Gaussian posterior and nested sparse variational learning. These choices make the proposed trajectory model more efficient and scalable to fit. Results in several real-world applications demonstrate its advantage. The central change is to make entity representations evolve over time, so temporal information shapes the decomposition itself rather than leaving the factors static.
summary.tldr: NONFAT learns evolving tensor-factor trajectories with Gaussian processes to capture temporal relationships in sparse data.

title: Nonparametric Factor Trajectory Learning for Dynamic Tensor Decomposition

abstract: Accurate probabilistic predictions are essential for optimal decision making. While neural network miscalibration has been studied primarily in classification, we investigate this in the less-explored domain of regression. We conduct the largest empirical study to date to assess the probabilistic calibration of neural networks. We also analyze the performance of recalibration, conformal, and regularization methods to enhance probabilistic calibration. Additionally, we introduce novel differentiable recalibration and regularization methods, uncovering new insights into their effectiveness. Our findings reveal that regularization methods offer a favorable tradeoff between calibration and sharpness. Post-hoc methods exhibit superior probabilistic calibration, which we attribute to the finite-sample coverage guarantee of conformal prediction. Furthermore, we demonstrate that quantile recalibration can be considered as a specific case of conformal prediction. Our study is fully reproducible and implemented in a common code base for fair comparisons.
