paragraphs: A regression model can predict a range of possible numerical outcomes rather than a single value. For these predictions to support decisions, their stated uncertainty needs to agree with what actually happens. This paper examines that agreement, called probabilistic calibration, in neural network regression, an area less studied than calibration in classification.

The authors conduct a large empirical comparison of methods that improve calibration through recalibration, conformal prediction, or regularization. These approaches adjust predictions or influence training in different ways. They also introduce differentiable recalibration and regularization methods, allowing calibration-related adjustments to participate in gradient-based optimization.

The findings distinguish calibration from sharpness: predictions should reflect uncertainty accurately while remaining informative. Regularization offers a favorable balance between these aims, whereas post-hoc methods achieve better probabilistic calibration in the study. The authors attribute this advantage to conformal prediction’s finite-sample coverage guarantee and show that quantile recalibration is a special case of conformal prediction. A shared, reproducible implementation supports fair comparisons between the methods.
summary.tldr: A large regression study compares calibration methods and connects quantile recalibration to conformal prediction.

title: A Large-Scale Study of Probabilistic Calibration in Neural Network Regression

abstract: As predictive models seep into several real-world applications, it has become critical to ensure that individuals who are negatively impacted by the outcomes of these models are provided with a means for recourse. To this end, there has been a growing body of research on algorithmic recourse in recent years. While recourses can be extremely beneficial to affected individuals, their implementation at a large scale can lead to potential data distribution shifts and other unintended consequences. However, there is little to no research on understanding the impact of algorithmic recourse after implementation. In this work, we address the aforementioned gaps by making one of the first attempts at analyzing the delayed societal impact of algorithmic recourse. To this end, we theoretically and empirically analyze the recourses output by state-of-the-art algorithms. Our analysis demonstrates that large-scale implementation of recourses by end users may exacerbate social segregation. To address this problem, we propose novel algorithms which leverage implicit and explicit conditional generative models to not only minimize the chance of segregation but also provide realistic recourses. Extensive experimentation with real-world datasets demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed approaches.

paragraphs: Algorithmic recourse gives people negatively affected by a predictive model a way to pursue a different outcome. Although such recommendations can help individuals, many people acting on them can change the overall data distribution. This paper examines the delayed societal consequences of implementing recourse at scale, focusing on social segregation.

The authors theoretically and empirically analyze recommendations produced by state-of-the-art recourse algorithms. Their analysis shows that widespread adoption may worsen segregation. This shifts attention from whether a recommendation helps one person to what happens when many recommendations are followed together. The reported risk is a possible aggregate consequence, rather than a claim that every recourse intervention increases segregation.

To address that risk, the paper proposes algorithms using implicit and explicit conditional generative models. The goal is to produce realistic recourses while minimizing the chance of segregation. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches. The work therefore connects the design of individual recommendations with their broader distributional effects and offers methods that account for both.
summary.tldr: Large-scale algorithmic recourse may increase social segregation; conditional generative approaches aim to reduce that risk while keeping recommendations realistic.

title: On the Impact of Algorithmic Recourse on Social Segregation

abstract: We study the connection between multicalibration and boosting for squared error regression. First we prove a useful characterization of multicalibration in terms of a “swap regret” like condition on squared error. Using this characterization, we give an exceedingly simple algorithm that can be analyzed both as a boosting algorithm for regression and as a multicalibration algorithm for a class $\mathcal{H}$ that makes use only of a standard squared error regression oracle for $\mathcal{H}$. We give a weak learning assumption on $\mathcal{H}$ that ensures convergence to Bayes optimality without the need to make any realizability assumptions — giving us an agnostic boosting algorithm for regression. We then show that our weak learning assumption on $\mathcal{H}$ is both necessary and sufficient for multicalibration with respect to $\mathcal{H}$ to imply Bayes optimality, answering an open question. We also show that if $\mathcal{H}$ satisfies our weak learning condition relative to another class $\mathcal{C}$ then multicalibration with respect to $\mathcal{H}$ implies multicalibration with respect to $\mathcal{C}$. Finally we investigate the empirical performance of our algorithm experimentally.

paragraphs: This paper connects multicalibration, a collection of prediction consistency requirements, with boosting for regression under squared error. The authors first characterize multicalibration through a condition resembling swap regret. This creates a bridge between satisfying calibration requirements and repeatedly improving a predictor's squared-error performance.

Using that characterization, they develop a simple algorithm that can be understood both as regression boosting and as multicalibration for a function class H. It requires only a standard squared-error regression oracle for that class. Under a stated weak learning assumption on H, the algorithm converges to Bayes-optimal prediction without assuming that the ideal prediction function belongs to the chosen model class.

The weak learning condition is central to the guarantee. The authors prove it is both necessary and sufficient for multicalibration with respect to H to imply Bayes optimality. They also show that an appropriate relative weak learning condition transfers multicalibration from H to another class C. Alongside these theoretical connections, the paper investigates the algorithm experimentally, bringing calibration and agnostic regression boosting into a shared framework.
summary.tldr: A shared algorithm links multicalibration and regression boosting, with Bayes-optimality guarantees governed by a necessary and sufficient weak learning condition.

title: Multicalibration as Boosting for Regression

abstract: Compositional reinforcement learning is a promising approach for training policies to perform complex long-horizon tasks. Typically, a high-level task is decomposed into a sequence of subtasks and a separate policy is trained to perform each subtask. In this paper, we focus on the problem of training subtask policies in a way that they can be used to perform any task; here, a task is given by a sequence of subtasks. We aim to maximize the worst-case performance over all tasks as opposed to the average-case performance. We formulate the problem as a two agent zero-sum game in which the adversary picks the sequence of subtasks. We propose two RL algorithms to solve this game: one is an adaptation of existing multi-agent RL algorithms to our setting and the other is an asynchronous version which enables parallel training of subtask policies. We evaluate our approach on two multi-task environments with continuous states and actions and demonstrate that our algorithms outperform state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Compositional reinforcement learning builds long tasks from sequences of smaller subtasks, each handled by its own policy. The challenge studied here is to train those policies so they remain useful across different task sequences. The authors focus on maximizing performance on the worst sequence, making robustness across compositions the training objective.

They formulate learning as a two-agent zero-sum game. One side learns the subtask policies, while an adversary selects the sequence of subtasks. This makes difficult compositions part of the optimization process. The paper proposes two algorithms: an adaptation of existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods and an asynchronous version that allows subtask policies to train in parallel.

Evaluation in two multi-task environments with continuous states and actions shows improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. These experiments support the proposed training strategy for producing more robust reusable components. The objective targets worst-case performance across tasks, while the reported empirical finding is improved performance in the two tested environments; it does not establish successful execution of every possible sequence.
summary.tldr: Adversarially choosing subtask sequences trains reusable reinforcement-learning policies toward stronger worst-case compositional performance.

title: Robust Subtask Learning for Compositional Generalization

abstract: Visualization is a crucial step in exploratory data analysis. One possible approach is to train an autoencoder with low-dimensional latent space. Large network depth and width can help unfolding the data. However, such expressive networks can achieve low reconstruction error even when the latent representation is distorted. To avoid such misleading visualizations, we propose first a differential geometric perspective on the decoder, leading to insightful diagnostics for an embedding’s distortion, and second a new regularizer mitigating such distortion. Our “Geometric Autoencoder” avoids stretching the embedding spuriously, so that the visualization captures the data structure more faithfully. It also flags areas where little distortion could not be achieved, thus guarding against misinterpretation.

paragraphs: An autoencoder can turn complex data into a low-dimensional representation suitable for plotting. However, a visually appealing plot and accurate reconstruction do not necessarily mean that the plotted geometry faithfully reflects the data. A sufficiently expressive decoder can reconstruct examples well even when their arrangement in the latent space is distorted.

The paper examines this problem through the differential geometry of the decoder. This perspective provides diagnostics for how the embedding stretches or distorts the represented data. The authors also introduce a regularizer that discourages such distortion during learning, producing what they call a Geometric Autoencoder. The objective is to improve the correspondence between the displayed embedding and what it decodes.

The resulting method avoids spurious stretching so that visualizations capture data structure more faithfully. It also flags regions where achieving low distortion was not possible. Those flags matter because a visualization can otherwise encourage unwarranted confidence in apparent geometric relationships. The approach combines an attempt to reduce distortion with a way to reveal where distortion remains.
summary.tldr: Geometric Autoencoders reduce misleading distortion in low-dimensional visualizations and flag regions where low distortion could not be achieved.

title: Geometric Autoencoders - What You See is What You Decode

abstract: Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is a powerful set of techniques for imitation learning that aims to learn a reward function that rationalizes expert demonstrations. Unfortunately, traditional IRL methods suffer from a computational weakness: they require repeatedly solving a hard reinforcement learning (RL) problem as a subroutine. This is counter-intuitive from the viewpoint of reductions: we have reduced the easier problem of imitation learning to repeatedly solving the harder problem of RL. Another thread of work has proved that access to the side-information of the distribution of states where a strong policy spends time can dramatically reduce the sample and computational complexities of solving an RL problem. In this work, we demonstrate for the first time a more informed imitation learning reduction where we utilize the state distribution of the expert to alleviate the global exploration component of the RL subroutine, providing an exponential speedup in theory. In practice, we find that we are able to significantly speed up the prior art on continuous control tasks.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks a reward function that explains expert demonstrations. Traditional approaches repeatedly solve reinforcement-learning problems as part of this process, making imitation computationally expensive. The paper questions this arrangement because learning to imitate is being handled through repeated calls to the harder problem of discovering good behavior through reinforcement learning.

The authors use additional information already connected to the expert: the distribution of states the expert visits. Their reduction uses this distribution to alleviate the global-exploration component of the reinforcement-learning subroutine. This builds on the observation that knowing where a strong policy spends time can substantially reduce the effort needed to solve a learning problem.

The resulting approach provides an exponential speedup in the theoretical analysis. Experiments on continuous-control tasks also show substantial speedups over prior methods. The key idea is that expert demonstrations can inform where learning should focus, as well as which behavior should be explained, reducing the computational burden of the imitation-learning procedure.
summary.tldr: Using the expert's state distribution reduces exploration costs in inverse reinforcement learning, yielding theoretical and practical speedups.

title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning without Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper focuses on continual meta-learning, where few-shot tasks are heterogeneous and sequentially available. Recent works use a mixture model for meta-knowledge to deal with the heterogeneity. However, these methods suffer from parameter inefficiency caused by two reasons: (1) the underlying assumption of mutual exclusiveness among mixture components hinders sharing meta-knowledge across heterogeneous tasks. (2) they only allow increasing mixture components and cannot adaptively filter out redundant components. In this paper, we propose an Adaptive Compositional Continual Meta-Learning (ACML) algorithm, which employs a compositional premise to associate a task with a subset of mixture components, allowing meta-knowledge sharing among heterogeneous tasks. Moreover, to adaptively adjust the number of mixture components, we propose a component sparsification method based on evidential theory to filter out redundant components. Experimental results show ACML outperforms strong baselines, showing the effectiveness of our compositional meta-knowledge, and confirming that ACML can adaptively learn meta-knowledge.

paragraphs: Continual meta-learning involves learning from a sequence of tasks, each with few examples, while developing knowledge useful for later tasks. When tasks differ substantially, mixture models can maintain different components of this shared knowledge. The paper identifies two sources of parameter inefficiency: treating components as mutually exclusive and allowing the collection to grow without removing redundancy.

Adaptive Compositional Continual Meta-Learning, or ACML, associates each task with a subset of components. This lets different tasks reuse overlapping combinations of knowledge. The compositional premise matters because heterogeneous tasks can still share useful elements, even when assigning them to a single exclusive component would obscure that overlap.

ACML also uses component sparsification based on evidential theory to filter out redundant components and adapt the number retained. Experiments show improvements over strong baselines and support the effectiveness of compositional meta-knowledge. The stated contribution combines two forms of adaptation: changing how tasks share existing knowledge and adjusting which components remain useful as tasks arrive.
summary.tldr: ACML shares combinations of meta-knowledge across sequential few-shot tasks and removes redundant components to adapt its capacity.

title: Adaptive Compositional Continual Meta-Learning

abstract: Recently, the newly emerged multimodal models, which leverage both visual and linguistic modalities to train powerful encoders, have gained increasing attention. However, learning from a large-scale unlabeled dataset also exposes the model to the risk of potential poisoning attacks, whereby the adversary aims to perturb the model’s training data to trigger malicious behaviors in it. In contrast to previous work, only poisoning visual modality, in this work, we take the first step to studying poisoning attacks against multimodal models in both visual and linguistic modalities. Specially, we focus on answering two questions: (1) Is the linguistic modality also vulnerable to poisoning attacks? and (2) Which modality is most vulnerable? To answer the two questions, we propose three types of poisoning attacks against multimodal models. Extensive evaluations on different datasets and model architectures show that all three attacks can achieve significant attack performance while maintaining model utility in both visual and linguistic modalities. Furthermore, we observe that the poisoning effect differs between different modalities. To mitigate the attacks, we propose both pre-training and post-training defenses. We empirically show that both defenses can significantly reduce the attack performance while preserving the model’s utility. Our code is available at https://github.com/zqypku/mm_poison/.

paragraphs: Multimodal encoders learn from both images and language, often using large unlabeled datasets. This creates an opportunity for data poisoning: altering training examples to induce unwanted model behavior. The paper investigates vulnerabilities in both modalities, extending the focus beyond attacks that modify only the visual side of training.

The authors propose three types of poisoning attacks to examine whether language is vulnerable and how poisoning effects differ across modalities. Evaluations across datasets and model architectures show substantial attack performance while preserving model utility in both vision and language. This means ordinary usefulness can coexist with the malicious behaviors induced by poisoned training data.

The paper also introduces defenses applied before training and after training. Both empirically reduce attack performance while preserving utility. The findings establish that poisoning is a concern across modalities and that its effect depends on the modality involved. The reported defenses mitigate the tested attacks; the results do not amount to a claim that all poisoning vulnerabilities are removed.
summary.tldr: Multimodal encoders are vulnerable to poisoning across image and language data, while proposed defenses reduce tested attacks without sacrificing utility.

title: Data Poisoning Attacks Against Multimodal Encoders

abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive performance in generating fluent and realistic text, controlling the generated text so that it exhibits properties such as safety, factuality, and non-toxicity remains challenging. Existing decoding-based controllable text generation methods are static in terms of the dimension of control; if the target subject is changed, they require new training. Moreover, it can quickly become prohibitive to concurrently control multiple subjects. To address these challenges, we first show that existing methods can be framed as a reinforcement learning problem, where an action-value function estimates the likelihood of a desired attribute appearing in the generated text. Then, we introduce a novel approach named SF-Gen, which leverages the concept of successor features to decouple the dynamics of LLMs from task-specific rewards. By employing successor features, our method proves to be memory-efficient and computationally efficient for both training and decoding, especially when dealing with multiple target subjects. To the best of our knowledge, our research represents the first application of successor features in text generation. In addition to its computational efficiency, the resultant language produced by our method is comparable to the SOTA (and outperforms baselines) in both control measures as well as language quality, which we demonstrate through a series of experiments in various controllable text generation tasks.

paragraphs: Controlling generated text becomes expensive when a system must handle changing or multiple target subjects. Existing decoding-based methods can require new training when the control target changes, and simultaneous controls can add substantial cost. SF-Gen addresses this by separating reusable information about language generation from the rewards associated with particular control goals.

The paper first expresses existing approaches as reinforcement learning problems. In this view, an action-value function estimates the likelihood that generated text will exhibit a desired attribute. SF-Gen then uses successor features to decouple the language model's dynamics from task-specific rewards, making the control framework less tightly tied to an individual target.

The authors report memory and computational efficiency during both training and decoding, especially with multiple subjects. Across controllable generation experiments, the method produces text comparable to state-of-the-art approaches in control and language quality, while outperforming baselines. The contribution combines a reusable representation for control with empirical evidence that improved efficiency can coexist with strong generated-text quality in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: SF-Gen separates language-generation dynamics from control rewards using successor features, improving efficiency for multiple target subjects.

title: Successor Features for Efficient Multi-Subject Controlled Text Generation

abstract: Graph neural networks based on iterative one-hop message passing have been shown to struggle in harnessing the information from distant nodes effectively. Conversely, graph transformers allow each node to attend to all other nodes directly, but lack graph inductive bias and have to rely on ad-hoc positional encoding. In this paper, we propose a new architecture to reconcile these challenges. Our approach stems from the recent breakthroughs in long-range modeling provided by deep state-space models: for a given target node, our model aggregates other nodes by their shortest distances to the target and uses a linear RNN to encode the sequence of hop representations. The linear RNN is parameterized in a particular diagonal form for stable long-range signal propagation and is theoretically expressive enough to encode the neighborhood hierarchy. With no need for positional encoding, we empirically show that the performance of our model is comparable to or better than that of state-of-the-art graph transformers on various benchmarks, with a significantly reduced computational cost. Our code is open-source at https://github.com/skeletondyh/GRED.

paragraphs: Graph models face a tension between capturing distant information and preserving the structure of the graph. Repeated one-hop message passing can struggle with distant nodes, while graph transformers allow direct interactions but rely on added positional information. This paper proposes an architecture that organizes long-range information using the graph’s own shortest-path distances.

For each target node, the model groups other nodes according to their distance from it and aggregates each group into a hop representation. A linear recurrent neural network then processes the resulting sequence. Its specially chosen diagonal parameterization supports stable propagation over long ranges, and the authors prove that it is expressive enough to encode the hierarchy of neighborhoods.

The model does not require positional encoding. Across several benchmarks, its measured performance matches or exceeds state-of-the-art graph transformers while using significantly less computation. The approach therefore provides an explicit way to combine distance-based graph structure with long-range sequence modeling, with theoretical support for representing neighborhood hierarchy and empirical support for its computational advantages.
summary.tldr: A linear recurrent model processes distance-grouped graph neighborhoods, matching or exceeding graph-transformer performance on benchmarks with substantially lower computation.

title: Recurrent Distance Filtering for Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Time series data, characterized by its intrinsic long and short-range dependencies, poses a unique challenge across analytical applications. While Transformer-based models excel at capturing long-range dependencies, they face limitations in noise sensitivity, computational efficiency, and overfitting with smaller datasets. In response, we introduce a novel Time Series Lightweight Adaptive Network (TSLANet), as a universal convolutional model for diverse time series tasks. Specifically, we propose an Adaptive Spectral Block, harnessing Fourier analysis to enhance feature representation and to capture both long-term and short-term interactions while mitigating noise via adaptive thresholding. Additionally, we introduce an Interactive Convolution Block and leverage self-supervised learning to refine the capacity of TSLANet for decoding complex temporal patterns and improve its robustness on different datasets. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that TSLANet outperforms state-of-the-art models in various tasks spanning classification, forecasting, and anomaly detection, showcasing its resilience and adaptability across a spectrum of noise levels and data sizes. The code is available at https://github.com/emadeldeen24/TSLANet.

The spectral component uses Fourier analysis to represent long-term and short-term interactions, while adaptive thresholding mitigates noise. The convolutional component and self-supervised learning further support learning complex temporal patterns. Together, these elements give the model several ways to represent temporal structure and improve robustness across datasets.

The authors evaluate classification, forecasting, and anomaly detection, reporting performance above state-of-the-art models in the experiments. They also examine different noise levels and data sizes, finding resilience across those conditions. These results support the proposed architecture as a broadly useful time-series representation model within the evaluated settings, with spectral processing and convolution contributing to its design.
summary.tldr: TSLANet combines adaptive spectral processing, convolution, and self-supervised learning for robust performance across several time-series tasks.

title: TSLANet: Rethinking Transformers for Time Series Representation Learning

abstract: We investigate the accuracy of prediction in deterministic learning dynamics of zero-sum games with random initializations, specifically focusing on observer uncertainty and its relationship to the evolution of covariances. Zero-sum games are a prominent field of interest in machine learning due to their various applications. Concurrently, the accuracy of prediction in dynamical systems from mechanics has long been a classic subject of investigation since the discovery of the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle. This principle employs covariance and standard deviation of particle states to measure prediction accuracy. In this study, we bring these two approaches together to analyze the Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL) algorithm in two-player zero-sum games. We provide growth rates of covariance information for continuous-time FTRL, as well as its two canonical discretization methods (Euler and Symplectic). A Heisenberg-type inequality is established for FTRL. Our analysis and experiments also show that employing Symplectic discretization enhances the accuracy of prediction in learning dynamics.

paragraphs: Even when a learning rule is deterministic, uncertainty about its starting point can make its future behavior difficult to predict. This paper studies that situation for Follow-the-Regularized-Leader, or FTRL, in two-player zero-sum games. It focuses on random initializations and how an observer's uncertainty evolves over time.

The authors describe uncertainty through covariance information, drawing a connection to methods used to study prediction accuracy in mechanics. They derive covariance growth rates for continuous-time FTRL and for two ways of turning it into discrete updates: Euler and symplectic discretization. They also establish a Heisenberg-type inequality for the learning dynamics.

Both the analysis and experiments indicate that symplectic discretization improves prediction accuracy. The result concerns how accurately an observer can forecast the learning trajectory, rather than simply whether players learn useful strategies. By comparing continuous and discrete dynamics through the same uncertainty-based perspective, the paper shows that the choice of numerical update scheme can affect the predictability of strategic learning.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes uncertainty in FTRL game-learning trajectories and finds that symplectic discretization improves their predictability.

title: Prediction Accuracy of Learning in Games : Follow-the-Regularized-Leader meets Heisenberg

abstract: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have shown remarkable performance in learning 3D scenes. However, NeRF exhibits vulnerability when confronted with distractors in the training images – unexpected objects are present only within specific views, such as moving entities like pedestrians or birds. Excluding distractors during dataset construction is a straightforward solution, but without prior knowledge of their types and quantities, it becomes prohibitively expensive. In this paper, we propose PruNeRF, a segment-centric dataset pruning framework via 3D spatial consistency, that effectively identifies and prunes the distractors. We first examine existing metrics for measuring pixel-wise distraction and introduce Influence Functions for more accurate measurements. Then, we assess 3D spatial consistency using a depth-based reprojection technique to obtain 3D-aware distraction. Furthermore, we incorporate segmentation for pixel-to-segment refinement, enabling more precise identification. Our experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that PruNeRF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in robustness against distractors.

paragraphs: Neural Radiance Fields learn a three-dimensional scene from images, but temporary objects can interfere with that reconstruction. A pedestrian or bird may appear in only some views, making the training images inconsistent. PruNeRF identifies and removes such distracting content without requiring advance knowledge of the distractors' types and quantities.

The method begins with pixel-level measurements of distraction, introducing influence functions to improve their accuracy. It then uses depth-based reprojection to assess consistency in three-dimensional space. This adds information about how observations relate across views, producing distraction estimates that account for the scene's geometry rather than treating pixels independently.

Finally, segmentation refines those pixel-level estimates into decisions about image regions. The combination of influence measurements, geometric consistency, and segment-level refinement is designed to identify distractors more precisely. On benchmark datasets, the authors report consistently greater robustness to distractors than existing leading methods. The contribution is a dataset-pruning framework that uses the shared three-dimensional scene to guide which training content should be excluded.
summary.tldr: PruNeRF combines influence measurements, 3D consistency, and segmentation to remove distracting training content and improve scene reconstruction robustness.

title: PruNeRF: Segment-Centric Dataset Pruning via 3D Spatial Consistency

abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) has emerged as a promising technique to reduce the cost of large language models (LLMs). Specifically, PTQ can effectively mitigate memory consumption and reduce computational overhead in LLMs. To meet the requirements of both high efficiency and performance across diverse scenarios, a comprehensive evaluation of quantized LLMs is essential to guide the selection of quantization methods. This paper presents a thorough evaluation of these factors by evaluating the effect of PTQ on Weight, Activation, and KV Cache on 11 model families, including OPT, LLaMA2, Falcon, Bloomz, Mistral, ChatGLM, Vicuna, LongChat, StableLM, Gemma, and Mamba, with parameters ranging from 125M to 180B. The evaluation encompasses five types of tasks: basic NLP, emergent ability, trustworthiness, dialogue, and long-context tasks. Moreover, we also evaluate the state-of-the-art (SOTA) quantization methods to demonstrate their applicability. Based on the extensive experiments, we systematically summarize the effect of quantization, provide recommendations to apply quantization techniques, and point out future directions. The code can be found in https://github.com/thu-nics/qllm-eval.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization can reduce the memory and computation required by large language models. Choosing how to apply it also requires understanding what happens to model performance across different uses. This paper conducts a broad evaluation intended to support that choice, examining quantization of weights, activations, and the key-value cache.

The evaluation covers 11 model families, with model sizes ranging from 125 million to 180 billion parameters. It spans five task categories: basic natural-language processing, emergent abilities, trustworthiness, dialogue, and long-context tasks. This breadth makes different aspects of model behavior part of the assessment, alongside the efficiency motivation for compression.

The authors also evaluate state-of-the-art quantization methods to assess their applicability. They use the experimental results to summarize quantization effects, develop recommendations, and identify future research directions. The contribution is a systematic evaluation spanning model families, sizes, quantized components, and task types. It provides an empirical basis for considering performance requirements across diverse scenarios when selecting a quantization technique.
summary.tldr: This study evaluates post-training quantization across 11 model families, three model components, and five task categories to inform method selection.

title: Evaluating Quantized Large Language Models

abstract: Leveraging second-order information about the loss at the scale of deep networks is one of the main lines of approach for improving the performance of current optimizers for deep learning. Yet, existing approaches for accurate full-matrix preconditioning, such as Full-Matrix Adagrad (GGT) or Matrix-Free Approximate Curvature (M-FAC) suffer from massive storage costs when applied even to small-scale models, as they must store a sliding window of gradients, whose memory requirements are multiplicative in the model dimension. In this paper, we address this issue via a novel and efficient error-feedback technique that can be applied to compress preconditioners by up to two orders of magnitude in practice, without loss of convergence. Specifically, our approach compresses the gradient information via sparsification or low-rank compression before it is fed into the preconditioner, feeding the compression error back into future iterations. Extensive experiments on deep neural networks show that this approach can compress full-matrix preconditioners to up to 99% sparsity without accuracy loss, effectively removing the memory overhead of fullmatrix preconditioners such as GGT and M-FAC.

paragraphs: Full-matrix preconditioners use information about the loss geometry to improve optimization updates. Methods such as GGT and M-FAC retain a sliding window of gradients to obtain this information. Because each stored gradient grows with the number of model parameters, the resulting memory requirement can become substantial even for relatively small neural networks.

The paper proposes compressing gradient information before it enters the preconditioner. It uses either sparsification, which retains fewer entries, or a low-rank representation. The key addition is error feedback: information lost during compression is carried forward into later iterations, giving subsequent updates a way to account for earlier compression errors.

The authors report compression of preconditioners by up to two orders of magnitude in practice without losing convergence. Experiments on deep networks also reach up to 99% sparsity without accuracy loss, effectively removing the reported memory overhead of these full-matrix methods. These findings support error feedback as a way to retain useful preconditioning information while greatly reducing the amount of gradient data that must be stored.
summary.tldr: Feeding compression errors into future iterations enables much smaller full-matrix preconditioners, reaching 99% sparsity without accuracy loss in experiments.

title: Error Feedback Can Accurately Compress Preconditioners

abstract: Despite extreme sample inefficiency, on-policy reinforcement learning, aka policy gradients, has become a fundamental tool in decision-making problems. With the recent advances in GPU-driven simulation, the ability to collect large amounts of data for RL training has scaled exponentially. However, we show that current RL methods, e.g. PPO, fail to ingest the benefit of parallelized environments beyond a certain point and their performance saturates. To address this, we propose a new on-policy RL algorithm that can effectively leverage large-scale environments by splitting them into chunks and fusing them back together via importance sampling. Our algorithm, termed SAPG, shows significantly higher performance across a variety of challenging environments where vanilla PPO and other strong baselines fail to achieve high performance. Webpage at https://sapg-rl.github.io/.

paragraphs: GPU-based simulation makes it possible to collect reinforcement-learning experience from many environments at once. However, increasing that parallelism does not automatically produce better learning. This paper reports that methods such as PPO eventually stop gaining much performance as the number of parallel environments grows.

The proposed Split and Aggregate Policy Gradients algorithm, or SAPG, changes how large-scale environment experience is organized. It splits the environments into chunks and combines them through importance sampling. This provides a way to aggregate the contributions of the chunks within an on-policy reinforcement-learning algorithm designed to benefit from large numbers of environments.

Across a range of challenging environments, the authors report substantially higher performance than vanilla PPO and other strong baselines that fail to attain high performance in those tests. The contribution addresses how an algorithm uses available parallel simulation, beyond simply making more experience available. Its findings show that changing the organization and aggregation of training experience can improve the benefits obtained from large-scale environments in the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: SAPG splits parallel environments into chunks and aggregates them with importance sampling, improving reported performance where PPO's scaling benefits saturate.

title: SAPG: Split and Aggregate Policy Gradients

abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) has been a popular method for uncertainty quantification because it is distribution-free, model-agnostic, and theoretically sound. For forecasting problems in supervised learning, most CP methods focus on building prediction intervals for univariate responses. In this work, we develop a sequential CP method called $\texttt{MultiDimSPCI}$ that builds prediction $\textit{regions}$ for a multivariate response, especially in the context of multivariate time series, which are not exchangeable. Theoretically, we estimate $\textit{finite-sample}$ high-probability bounds on the conditional coverage gap. Empirically, we demonstrate that $\texttt{MultiDimSPCI}$ maintains valid coverage on a wide range of multivariate time series while producing smaller prediction regions than CP and non-CP baselines.

paragraphs: Forecasting several quantities at once requires uncertainty estimates for their joint outcome. A separate interval for one response does not itself describe the full multivariate result. This paper introduces MultiDimSPCI, a sequential conformal prediction method that constructs ellipsoidal prediction regions for multivariate responses, with particular attention to time series.

Time series create a challenge because their observations are not exchangeable: temporal ordering and dependence matter. The theoretical contribution is a finite-sample, high-probability bound on the conditional coverage gap. This quantifies uncertainty about how closely conditional coverage approaches its target, rather than asserting that conditional coverage is always exactly correct.

Experiments show valid coverage across a wide range of evaluated multivariate time series, alongside smaller prediction regions than the compared conformal and non-conformal baselines. Smaller regions are useful when they retain coverage because they narrow the range of plausible joint outcomes. The contribution combines sequential multivariate uncertainty estimation with theoretical coverage analysis and empirical evidence of more compact regions.
summary.tldr: MultiDimSPCI builds compact multivariate time-series prediction regions with finite-sample bounds on the conditional coverage gap.

title: Conformal prediction for multi-dimensional time series by ellipsoidal sets

abstract: Large models training is plagued by the intense compute cost and limited hardware memory. A practical solution is low-precision representation but is troubled by loss in numerical accuracy and unstable training rendering the model less useful. We argue that low-precision floating points can perform well provided the error is properly compensated at the critical locations in the training process. We propose Collage which utilizes multi-component float representation in low-precision to accurately perform operations with numerical errors accounted. To understand the impact of imprecision to training, we propose a simple and novel metric which tracks the lost information during training as well as differentiates various precision strategies. Our method works with commonly used low-precision such as half-precision ($16$-bit floating points) and can be naturally extended to work with even lower precision such as $8$-bit. Experimental results show that pre-training using Collage removes the requirement of using $32$-bit floating-point copies of the model and attains similar/better training performance compared to $(16, 32)$-bit mixed-precision strategy, with up to $3.7\times$ speedup and $\sim 15%$ to $23%$ less memory usage in practice. The code is available at https://github.com/amazon-science/collage.

paragraphs: Training large language models requires substantial computation and memory. Lower-precision numbers can reduce those demands, but numerical errors can destabilize training or reduce its effectiveness. Collage addresses this problem by compensating for errors at important points in the training process, allowing low-precision arithmetic to preserve more useful information.

Its mechanism represents values using multiple low-precision floating-point components and accounts for numerical errors during operations. The authors also introduce a metric that tracks information lost during training and distinguishes different precision strategies. Collage works with 16-bit floating-point numbers, and the proposed approach can be extended to lower precision such as 8-bit.

It achieves similar or better training performance than a mixed 16-bit and 32-bit strategy, with speedups reaching 3.7 times and memory reductions of approximately 15% to 23%. These results support targeted error compensation as a way to obtain practical resource savings without the observed training penalties of uncompensated low precision.
summary.tldr: Collage compensates for low-precision numerical errors to train large models without 32-bit model copies, reducing measured runtime and memory use.

title: Collage: Light-Weight Low-Precision Strategy for LLM Training

abstract: Designing privacy-preserving DL solutions is a major challenge within the AI community. Homomorphic Encryption (HE) has emerged as one of the most promising approaches in this realm, enabling the decoupling of knowledge between a model owner and a data owner. Despite extensive research and application of this technology, primarily in CNNs, applying HE on transformer models has been challenging because of the difficulties in converting these models into a polynomial form. We break new ground by introducing the first polynomial transformer, providing the first demonstration of secure inference over HE with full transformers. This includes a transformer architecture tailored for HE, alongside a novel method for converting operators to their polynomial equivalent. This innovation enables us to perform secure inference on LMs and ViTs with several datasts and tasks. Our techniques yield results comparable to traditional models, bridging the performance gap with transformers of similar scale and underscoring the viability of HE for state-of-the-art applications. Finally, we assess the stability of our models and conduct a series of ablations to quantify the contribution of each model component. Our code is publicly available.

paragraphs: Homomorphic encryption offers a way to run model computations while separating what the model owner and data owner know. Applying it to transformers has been difficult because the models must be converted into a compatible polynomial form. This paper addresses that architectural and mathematical obstacle, extending an approach previously studied mainly with convolutional neural networks.

The authors introduce a transformer architecture tailored to homomorphic encryption and a method for converting its operators into polynomial equivalents. They present this as the first polynomial transformer and the first demonstration of secure inference with complete transformers under homomorphic encryption. Their evaluation includes both language models and vision transformers across several datasets and tasks.

The resulting models achieve performance comparable to traditional transformers of similar scale. The authors also examine stability and use ablations to assess how individual components contribute. These findings support the viability of converting whole transformer models into an encrypted-inference-compatible form while retaining useful task performance. The contribution combines an executable architecture with a conversion method, addressing the model as a complete computational system.
summary.tldr: A polynomial transformer architecture enables secure homomorphic-encryption inference with reported performance comparable to similarly sized conventional transformers.

title: Converting Transformers to Polynomial Form for Secure Inference Over Homomorphic Encryption

abstract: Resilience against malicious participants and data privacy are essential for trustworthy federated learning, yet achieving both with good utility typically requires the strong assumption of a trusted central server. This paper shows that a significantly weaker assumption suffices: each pair of participants shares a randomness seed unknown to others. In a setting where malicious participants may collude with an untrusted server, we propose CafCor, an algorithm that integrates robust gradient aggregation with correlated noise injection, using shared randomness between participants. We prove that CafCor achieves strong privacy-utility trade-offs, significantly outperforming local differential privacy (DP) methods, which do not make any trust assumption, while approaching central DP utility, where the server is fully trusted. Empirical results on standard benchmarks validate CafCor’s practicality, showing that privacy and robustness can coexist in distributed systems without sacrificing utility or trusting the server.

paragraphs: Federated learning needs to protect participants' data while resisting malicious contributions. Achieving both with strong model utility commonly assumes a trusted central server. This paper shows that a weaker trust arrangement can suffice: every pair of participants shares a random seed that remains unknown to everyone else.

The proposed algorithm, CafCor, combines robust gradient aggregation with correlated noise generated using those shared seeds. Robust aggregation addresses malicious updates, while the noise mechanism supports privacy. The analysis allows malicious participants to cooperate with an untrusted server, so server trust is not part of the assumed protection.

The authors prove privacy–utility trade-offs that substantially improve on local differential privacy methods, which make no trust assumption, while approaching the utility of central differential privacy with a fully trusted server. Experiments on standard benchmarks support the method's practicality. The result identifies pairwise secret randomness as a useful middle ground: it supplies enough additional structure to combine privacy and robustness with strong utility in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: CafCor uses pairwise secret randomness to combine privacy and malicious-participant robustness without trusting the federated-learning server.

title: Towards Trustworthy Federated Learning with Untrusted Participants

abstract: Mathematical optimization is fundamental to decision-making across diverse domains, from operations research to healthcare. Yet, translating real-world problems into optimization models remains a difficult task, often demanding specialized expertise. This paper approaches the problem of $\textit{autoformulation}$: the automated creation of solver-ready optimization models from natural language problem descriptions. We identify three core challenges of autoformulation: $\textit{(1)}$ the vast, problem-dependent hypothesis space, $\textit{(2)}$ efficient and diverse exploration of this space under uncertainty, and $\textit{(3)}$ evaluation of formulation correctness against problem description. To address these challenges, we present a novel method leveraging $\textit{Large Language Models}$ (LLMs) with $\textit{Monte-Carlo Tree Search}$, exploiting the hierarchical nature of optimization modeling to generate and systematically explore possible formulations. To enhance search efficiency, we introduce symbolic pruning to eliminate trivially equivalent search paths (branches), and employ LLM-based evaluation of partial formulations to guide search. Empirical analysis on linear and mixed-integer programming benchmarks demonstrates our method’s effectiveness, with significant performance gains from both LLM-based value estimation and symbolic pruning techniques.

paragraphs: Turning a written problem into a mathematical optimization model requires deciding how to express the problem in a form a solver can use. This paper studies automatic formulation from natural language. The challenge involves a large space of possible models, uncertainty about which possibilities to explore, and the need to assess whether a formulation matches the original description.

The method combines an LLM with Monte-Carlo Tree Search, organizing candidate formulations around the hierarchical structure of optimization modeling. Search explores alternative modeling choices, while LLM-based assessments of incomplete formulations help direct attention toward promising branches. This lets the system evaluate its progress before a complete candidate model has been assembled.

The authors also introduce symbolic pruning to remove branches that represent trivially equivalent alternatives, reducing redundant exploration. Experiments on linear and mixed-integer programming benchmarks demonstrate the method’s effectiveness and show significant gains from both pruning and LLM-based value estimation. These results support treating formulation as a structured search problem with guidance at intermediate stages.
summary.tldr: Combining LLM guidance, tree search, and symbolic pruning improves automatic construction of optimization models from written descriptions.

title: Autoformulation of Mathematical Optimization Models Using LLMs

abstract: Generative modeling typically concerns transporting a single source distribution to a target distribution via simple probability flows. However, in fields like computer graphics and single-cell genomics, samples themselves can be viewed as distributions, where standard flow matching ignores their inherent geometry. We propose Wasserstein flow matching (WFM), which lifts flow matching onto families of distributions using the Wasserstein geometry. Notably, WFM is the first algorithm capable of generating distributions in high dimensions, whether represented analytically (as Gaussians) or empirically (as point-clouds). Our theoretical analysis establishes that Wasserstein geodesics constitute proper conditional flows over the space of distributions, making for a valid FM objective. paragraphs: Ordinary generative modeling transports samples from a source distribution toward a target distribution. In some applications, however, each object being generated is itself a distribution, such as a point cloud describing a shape. Wasserstein flow matching extends flow matching to families of these objects, using Wasserstein geometry to respect their distributional structure.

The theoretical contribution establishes that Wasserstein geodesics provide valid conditional flows over the space of distributions. This supplies a foundation for the training objective. The algorithm combines optimal transport with attention and handles two representations: Gaussian distributions, for which it uses closed-form transport paths, and general distributions represented by point clouds, for which it uses entropic estimates.

The method generates two- and three-dimensional shapes as well as high-dimensional cellular microenvironments from spatial transcriptomics data. These demonstrations show its reach across different representations and dimensionalities. The key contribution is making distributions themselves the units of generation, with a flow construction that incorporates their geometry instead of treating their internal structure as incidental.
summary.tldr: Wasserstein flow matching generates whole distributions by extending flow matching to their optimal-transport geometry.

title: Wasserstein Flow Matching: Generative Modeling Over Families of Distributions

abstract: Cyclic peptides, characterized by geometric constraints absent in linear peptides, offer enhanced biochemical properties, presenting new opportunities to address unmet medical needs. However, designing target-specific cyclic peptides remains underexplored due to limited training data. To bridge the gap, we propose CP-Composer, a novel generative framework that enables zero-shot cyclic peptide generation via composable geometric constraints. Our approach decomposes complex cyclization patterns into unit constraints, which are incorporated into a diffusion model through geometric conditioning on nodes and edges. During training, the model learns from unit constraints and their random combinations in linear peptides, while at inference, novel constraint combinations required for cyclization are imposed as input. Experiments show that our model, despite trained with linear peptides, is capable of generating diverse target-binding cyclic peptides, reaching success rates from 38% to 84% on different cyclization strategies.

paragraphs: Cyclic peptides have geometric constraints that linear peptides do not, creating a challenge for generative design when cyclic training examples are scarce. CP-Composer addresses this by learning reusable geometric constraints from linear peptides and combining them to generate cyclic structures targeted toward binding.

During training, it sees unit constraints and random combinations within linear peptides. At inference, it receives new combinations that impose the requirements for cyclization, allowing the desired geometry to be specified through composed constraints.

Experiments show that a model trained on linear peptides can generate diverse target-binding cyclic peptides, with success rates ranging from 38% to 84% across different cyclization strategies. The zero-shot result concerns applying learned constraints in new combinations required for cyclic design. It supports compositional geometry as a way to transfer from available linear-peptide training data to a design setting with limited dedicated data.
summary.tldr: CP-Composer combines geometric constraints learned from linear peptides to generate target-binding cyclic peptides without cyclic-peptide training.

title: Zero-Shot Cyclic Peptide Design via Composable Geometric Constraints

abstract: Long-term time series forecasting has been widely studied, yet two aspects remain insufficiently explored: the interaction learning between different frequency components and the exploitation of periodic characteristics inherent in timestamps. To address the above issues, we propose CFPT, a novel method that empowering time series forecasting through Cross-Frequency Interaction (CFI) and Periodic-Aware Timestamp Modeling (PTM). To learn cross-frequency interactions, we design the CFI branch to process signals in frequency domain and captures their interactions through a feature fusion mechanism. Furthermore, to enhance prediction performance by leveraging timestamp periodicity, we develop the PTM branch which transforms timestamp sequences into 2D periodic tensors and utilizes 2D convolution to capture both intra-period dependencies and inter-period correlations of time series based on timestamp patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks demonstrate that CFPT achieves state-of-the-art performance in long-term forecasting tasks. The code is publicly available at this repository: https://github.com/BUPT-SN/CFPT.

paragraphs: CFPT targets two sources of information that the authors identify as insufficiently explored in long-term forecasting: relationships between frequency components and recurring patterns in timestamps. Its design treats these as complementary forecasting inputs. One describes interactions within the signal's frequency representation, while the other describes how observations are organized in recurring periods.

The cross-frequency interaction branch processes signals in the frequency domain and combines their features to learn relationships between components. The periodic-aware timestamp branch reshapes timestamp sequences into two-dimensional periodic tensors. It then applies two-dimensional convolution to capture dependencies within a period and correlations across periods, using the timestamp patterns as the organizing structure.

This combination matters because the forecasting model can use both interacting frequency information and repeated temporal organization. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world benchmarks report state-of-the-art long-term forecasting performance. Those results support the combined CFPT approach on the evaluated tasks; the abstract presents the two branches as its main methodological contributions without assigning a separate numerical gain to either one.
summary.tldr: CFPT combines cross-frequency feature interactions with periodic timestamp modeling to achieve state-of-the-art results on long-term forecasting benchmarks.

title: CFPT: Empowering Time Series Forecasting through Cross-Frequency Interaction and Periodic-Aware Timestamp Modeling

abstract: Despite their remarkable capabilities, large language models often struggle with tasks requiring complex reasoning and planning. While existing approaches like Chain-of-Thought prompting and tree search techniques show promise, they are limited by their reliance on predefined heuristics and computationally expensive exploration strategies. We propose Policy-Guided Tree Search (PGTS), a framework that combines reinforcement learning with structured tree exploration to efficiently navigate reasoning paths. Our key innovation is a learned policy that dynamically decides between expanding, branching, backtracking, or terminating exploration, eliminating the need for manual heuristics or exhaustive search. Experiments across mathematical reasoning, logical deduction, and planning benchmarks demonstrate that PGTS achieves superior reasoning performance while significantly reducing computational costs compared to existing methods. These results establish PGTS as a scalable and effective solution for tackling complex reasoning tasks with LLMs.

paragraphs: Language models can struggle with reasoning and planning tasks that require exploring multiple possible steps. Chain-of-thought prompting and tree search offer ways to organize this work, but predefined exploration rules can be restrictive, and extensive search can be costly. This paper asks how a model can learn to control the search process itself.

Policy-Guided Tree Search combines reinforcement learning with a tree of possible reasoning paths. A learned policy dynamically chooses whether to expand the current path, create a branch, backtrack, or stop. These decisions determine where additional reasoning effort is spent and when exploration should end, replacing manually specified search heuristics within the framework.

Experiments cover mathematical reasoning, logical deduction, and planning. The authors report better reasoning performance alongside substantially lower computational cost than the compared approaches. The findings support learned search control as a useful component of LLM reasoning: the framework improves both the exploration decisions and the efficiency with which candidate reasoning paths are examined.
summary.tldr: PGTS learns when to expand, branch, backtrack, or stop a reasoning search, improving tested reasoning performance while reducing computation.

title: Policy Guided Tree Search for Enhanced LLM Reasoning

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn an effective policy from a static dataset. To alleviate extrapolation errors, existing studies often uniformly regularize the value function or policy updates across all states. However, due to substantial variations in data quality, the fixed regularization strength often leads to a dilemma: Weak regularization strength fails to address extrapolation errors and value overestimation, while strong regularization strength shifts policy learning toward behavior cloning, impeding potential performance enabled by Bellman updates. To address this issue, we propose the selective state-adaptive regularization method for offline RL. Specifically, we introduce state-adaptive regularization coefficients to trust state-level Bellman-driven results, while selectively applying regularization on high-quality actions, aiming to avoid performance degradation caused by tight constraints on low-quality actions. By establishing a connection between the representative value regularization method, CQL, and explicit policy constraint methods, we effectively extend selective state-adaptive regularization to these two mainstream offline RL approaches. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches in both offline and offline-to-online settings on the D4RL benchmark. The implementation is available at https://github.com/QinwenLuo/SSAR.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns a policy from a fixed dataset, where the quality of available experience can vary substantially between states. Uniform regularization creates a difficult compromise. Weak constraints can permit extrapolation errors and inflated value estimates, while strong constraints can make the policy mostly imitate the recorded behavior and suppress improvements from Bellman updates.

The proposed method varies regularization strength by state, adjusting how much to trust the results of Bellman-driven learning. It also applies regularization selectively to high-quality actions, aiming to avoid constraining the policy tightly around low-quality behavior. Together, these choices make the constraints sensitive to both where the agent is and which recorded actions are worth preserving.

The authors connect conservative Q-learning with explicit policy constraints, extending their approach to both value-regularized and policy-constrained offline learning. Experiments on D4RL report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods in offline and offline-to-online settings. The findings support adapting constraints to the data’s uneven quality instead of imposing the same restriction everywhere.
summary.tldr: Selective state-adaptive regularization adjusts offline RL constraints by state and action quality, improving reported D4RL results.

title: Learning to Trust Bellman Updates: Selective State-Adaptive Regularization for Offline RL

abstract: We investigate the distance function learned by message passing neural networks (MPNNs) in specific tasks, aiming to capture the functional distance between prediction targets that MPNNs implicitly learn. This contrasts with previous work, which links MPNN distances on arbitrary tasks to structural distances on graphs that ignore task-specific information. To address this gap, we distill the distance between MPNN embeddings into an interpretable graph distance. Our method uses optimal transport on the Weisfeiler Leman Labeling Tree (WILT), where the edge weights reveal subgraphs that strongly influence the distance between embeddings. This approach generalizes two well-known graph kernels and can be computed in linear time. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that MPNNs define the relative position of embeddings by focusing on a small set of subgraphs that are known to be functionally important in the domain.

paragraphs: This paper asks what the distance between graph representations learned by a message passing neural network actually reflects. Earlier work relates such distances to graph structure without considering the prediction task. The authors instead investigate functional similarity: the task-relevant distinctions that shape how the network positions graphs in its representation space.

Their method distills distances between network embeddings into an interpretable graph distance. It uses optimal transport on a Weisfeiler Leman Labeling Tree, or WILT. The tree’s edge weights indicate which subgraphs strongly influence the distance, providing a way to inspect the features behind the network’s learned notion of similarity.

The resulting approach generalizes two established graph kernels and can be computed in linear time. Across extensive experiments, the authors find that the networks position embeddings using a small set of subgraphs known to be functionally important in the relevant domain. This connects learned representation geometry to recognizable domain features. The contribution is an explanation of task-specific distances, making it possible to examine why particular graphs are represented as relatively close or far apart.
summary.tldr: WILT-based distances explain graph-network embedding geometry through a small set of task-relevant subgraphs.

title: WILTing Trees: Interpreting the Distance Between MPNN Embeddings

abstract: We define the local complexity of a neural network with continuous piecewise linear activations as a measure of the density of linear regions over an input data distribution. We show theoretically that ReLU networks that learn low-dimensional feature representations have a lower local complexity. This allows us to connect recent empirical observations on feature learning at the level of the weight matrices with concrete properties of the learned functions. In particular, we show that the local complexity serves as an upper bound on the total variation of the function over the input data distribution and thus that feature learning can be related to adversarial robustness. Lastly, we consider how optimization drives ReLU networks towards solutions with lower local complexity. Overall, this work contributes a theoretical framework towards relating geometric properties of ReLU networks to different aspects of learning such as feature learning and representation cost.

This paper introduces local complexity to measure how densely those regions occur over an input data distribution. The distribution matters: the measure describes complexity in relation to the inputs being considered, rather than treating all parts of input space equally.

The authors prove that ReLU networks learning low-dimensional feature representations have lower local complexity. This connects properties of learned weight matrices to the geometry of the functions those networks implement. It provides a theoretical link between learning a compact representation and producing a function with less local regional complexity.

The paper further shows that local complexity upper-bounds the function’s total variation over the input distribution, establishing a route for relating feature learning to adversarial robustness. It also considers how optimization pushes networks toward lower-complexity solutions. The contribution is a framework connecting representation learning, functional variation, and network geometry, with robustness appearing through the stated theoretical relationship.
summary.tldr: A measure of local linear-region density links low-dimensional ReLU representations to functional variation and adversarial robustness.

title: On the Local Complexity of Linear Regions in Deep ReLU Networks

abstract: We introduce Interactive Bayesian Distributional Robustness (IBDR), a novel Bayesian inference framework that allows modeling the interactions between particles, thereby enhancing ensemble quality through increased particle diversity. IBDR is grounded in a generalized theoretical framework that connects the distributional population loss with the approximate posterior, motivating a practical dual optimization procedure that enforces distributional robustness while fostering particle diversity. We evaluate IBDR’s performance against various baseline methods using the VTAB-1K benchmark and the common reasoning language task. The results consistently show that IBDR outperforms these baselines, underscoring its effectiveness in real-world applications.

paragraphs: Interactive Bayesian Distributional Robustness, or IBDR, is a Bayesian inference framework aimed at improving ensembles when fine-tuning foundation models. It explicitly models interactions between particles, the members used in its ensemble representation. Those interactions promote greater particle diversity, which the paper connects to improved ensemble quality.

The framework’s theoretical basis relates distributional population loss to an approximate posterior. From this relationship, the authors motivate a practical dual optimization procedure that pursues distributional robustness while encouraging diversity. Robustness and interactions among particles are therefore built into the same inference approach. The method makes the relationships between ensemble members part of the optimization problem.

The authors evaluate IBDR against baseline methods on VTAB-1K and a common reasoning language task. They report consistent improvements over the compared methods. These findings support the practical value of encouraging particle diversity through the proposed Bayesian robustness framework across the evaluated tasks. The contribution combines a theoretical connection between loss and posterior approximation with an optimization procedure and empirical evidence for improved ensemble performance.
summary.tldr: IBDR models interactions among Bayesian ensemble particles to promote diversity and improve foundation-model fine-tuning.

title: Promoting Ensemble Diversity with Interactive Bayesian Distributional Robustness for Fine-tuning Foundation Models

abstract: Deep learning has become the de facto approach in nearly all learning tasks. It has been observed that deep models tend to memorize and sometimes overfit data, which can lead to compromises in performance, privacy, and other critical metrics. In this paper, we explore the theoretical foundations that connect memorization to sample loss, focusing on learning dynamics to understand what and how deep models memorize. To this end, we introduce a novel proxy for memorization: Cumulative Sample Loss (CSL). CSL represents the accumulated loss of a sample throughout the training process. CSL exhibits remarkable similarity to stability-based memorization, as evidenced by considerably high cosine similarity scores. We delve into the theory behind these results, demonstrating that low CSL leads to nontrivial bounds on the extent of stability-based memorization and learning time. The proposed proxy, CSL, is four orders of magnitude less computationally expensive than the stability-based method and can be obtained with zero additional overhead during training. We demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed proxy in identifying mislabeled samples and detecting duplicates where our metric achieves state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Understanding which examples a model memorizes can help investigate data quality, privacy, and generalization. This paper introduces Cumulative Sample Loss, or CSL, as a computationally inexpensive proxy for memorization. For each training example, CSL accumulates its loss throughout training, capturing its learning history rather than only its loss at the end.

The authors find high cosine similarity between CSL and stability-based memorization estimates. They also establish theoretical connections: low CSL implies nontrivial bounds on stability-based memorization and learning time. The contribution makes memorization-related analysis accessible through information already generated during training, while retaining the distinction between a proxy and the underlying memorization measure.
summary.tldr: Cumulative Sample Loss offers a cheap, theoretically supported proxy for memorization and performs strongly at identifying mislabeled and duplicate examples.

title: Towards Memorization Estimation: Fast, Formal and Free

abstract: Exploration is a cornerstone of reinforcement learning (RL). Intrinsic motivation attempts to decouple exploration from external, task-based rewards. However, established approaches to intrinsic motivation that follow general principles such as information gain, often only uncover low-level interactions. In contrast, children’s play suggests that they engage in meaningful high-level behavior by imitating or interacting with their caregivers. Recent work has focused on using foundation models to inject these semantic biases into exploration. However, these methods often rely on unrealistic assumptions, such as language-embedded environments or access to high-level actions. We propose SEmaNtically Sensible ExploratIon (SENSEI), a framework to equip model-based RL agents with an intrinsic motivation for semantically meaningful behavior. SENSEI distills a reward signal of interestingness from Vision Language Model (VLM) annotations, enabling an agent to predict these rewards through a world model. Using model-based RL, SENSEI trains an exploration policy that jointly maximizes semantic rewards and uncertainty. We show that in both robotic and video game-like simulations SENSEI discovers a variety of meaningful behaviors from image observations and low-level actions. SENSEI provides a general tool for learning from foundation model feedback, a crucial research direction, as VLMs become more powerful.

summary.tldr: SENSEI turns vision-language-model feedback into intrinsic rewards that guide meaningful exploration from images and low-level actions.

title: SENSEI: Semantic Exploration Guided by Foundation Models to Learn Versatile World Models

abstract: Optimal prompt selection is crucial for maximizing large language model (LLM) performance on downstream tasks, especially in black-box settings where models are only accessible via APIs. Black-box prompt selection is challenging due to potentially large, combinatorial search spaces, absence of gradient information, and high evaluation cost of prompts on a validation set. We propose HbBoPs, a novel method that combines a structural-aware deep kernel Gaussian Process with Hyperband as a multi-fidelity scheduler to efficiently select prompts. HbBoPs uses embeddings of instructions and few-shot exemplars, treating them as modular components within prompts. This enhances the surrogate model’s ability to predict which prompt to evaluate next in a sample-efficient manner. Hyperband improves query-efficiency by adaptively allocating resources across different fidelity levels, reducing the number of validation instances required for evaluating prompts. Extensive experiments across ten diverse benchmarks and three LLMs demonstrate that HbBoPs outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both performance and efficiency.
