paragraphs: Generating a SQL query is only part of enterprise data engineering; developers must also diagnose and repair complex queries that fail. This paper introduces Squirrel Benchmark to evaluate that debugging ability. It separates syntax problems, where an explicit error message is available, from semantic problems, where the code does not accomplish the user’s intended task.

The benchmark uses an automated workflow that reverse engineers SQL and injects realistic bugs, making it possible to construct varied examples at scale. Its evaluation framework assesses repairs without executing the queries. Squirrel contains 469 syntax queries and 516 semantic queries, averaging more than 140 lines, with broad and deeply nested syntax trees that reflect substantial structural complexity.

Across nearly 30 evaluated models, the strongest reported model, Claude-4-Sonnet, reaches 36.46% accuracy on syntax debugging and 32.17% on semantic debugging; most models remain below 20%. These results show a substantial performance gap on the benchmark’s enterprise debugging tasks. The authors also investigate four solution strategies to identify difficulties and possible directions for improving this capability.
summary.tldr: Squirrel Benchmark exposes major weaknesses in LLM debugging of complex enterprise SQL, with the best evaluated model solving roughly one-third of queries.

title: Beyond Text-to-SQL: Can LLMs Really Debug Enterprise ETL SQL?

abstract: Although reinforcement learning (RL) enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), it is primarily learned from the model’s self-generated distribution, limiting its ability to acquire reasoning skills beyond its initial knowledge. To overcome this, we propose a Difficulty-Aware Learning Strategy Allocation (DALSA) framework, which adaptively assigns appropriate learning strategies to samples based on their difficulty signals. DALSA is built on the key insight that samples beyond models’ knowledge scope are better addressed through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while those within the boundary but insufficiently mastered benefit more from RL, and well-learned samples are discarded to avoid redundant updates. To realize this principle, we extract a series of difficulty-aware training characteristics and employ a learnable strategy allocator to dynamically determine the optimal learning strategy for each sample based on its training dynamics. The allocator and the LLM are alternately optimized, enabling adaptive strategy allocation. Furthermore, two regularization techniques, anti-curriculum weighting and adversarial label smoothing, are integrated to alleviate the inherent limitations of RL and SFT, backed by comprehensive theoretical analyses. Extensive experiments on ten LLMs ranging from 1.5B to 70B across various tasks indicate that DALSA consistently outperforms baselines under both full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning settings.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often trains a language model on its own generated outputs, which can limit acquisition of reasoning skills beyond its initial knowledge. DALSA addresses this by choosing how to learn from each sample according to difficulty. Its organizing idea is that different relationships between a sample and the model’s current abilities call for different training strategies.

Samples beyond the model’s knowledge are assigned to supervised fine-tuning, while samples within reach but not yet mastered are assigned to reinforcement learning. Well-learned samples are discarded to avoid redundant updates. A learnable allocator makes these decisions from difficulty-related training characteristics, and the allocator and language model are optimized alternately as learning progresses.

The framework also includes anti-curriculum weighting and adversarial label smoothing, supported by theoretical analyses, to address limitations of the two training methods. Experiments on ten models spanning 1.5 billion to 70 billion parameters report consistent improvements over baselines across tasks in both full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. The findings support adapting the learning strategy to the model’s changing needs at the sample level.
summary.tldr: DALSA dynamically assigns samples to supervised learning, reinforcement learning, or skipping based on their difficulty relative to the model.

title: Tailoring the Training: Difficulty-Aware Learning Strategy Allocation for Large Language Models

abstract: This position paper argues that the absence of labels does not imply the absence of human supervision in visual learning, and urges the research community to identify sources of supervision more explicitly. Many recent methods in computer vision build upon representations learned from large-scale unlabeled data, and are therefore grouped under the same umbrella term "unsupervised." However, different data curation schemes and training objectives embed substantially different human priors on which models rely, and we argue that one "unsupervised" umbrella term is no longer capturing these distinctions. This ambiguity makes it harder to compare unsupervised learning research conducted under different assumptions, coinciding with a sharp decline in papers titled with "unsupervised" in flagship computer vision conferences since 2021, despite continued growth of the field. While we fully embrace pre-training as a strong foundation for modern computer vision, we advocate for a community-level effort toward greater conceptual clarity: authors are encouraged to disclose priors in data selection and learning objectives, and to specify which components of a learning pipeline depend on which assumptions. Standardized disclosure practices can improve academic communication, ensure fairer comparisons, and preserve methodological diversity in unsupervised learning.

paragraphs: This paper argues that unlabeled visual data can still carry substantial human supervision. Decisions about which data to collect or select and which training objectives to use embed human assumptions. Grouping all such methods under the term unsupervised can hide differences in the information and prior beliefs that their models rely on.

The authors connect this ambiguity to difficulties comparing research conducted under different assumptions. They also note a sharp decline since 2021 in papers with unsupervised in their titles at major vision conferences, despite continued growth of the field. This trend accompanies the conceptual problem; the abstract does not establish that the ambiguity caused the decline.

The proposal is to disclose the priors embedded in data selection and learning objectives and identify which pipeline components depend on which assumptions. The authors explicitly support pretraining as a foundation for modern vision. Their aim is clearer reporting around it, so researchers can compare methods more fairly, communicate their contributions more precisely, and preserve diversity in approaches to learning from unlabeled data.
summary.tldr: Visual-learning papers should disclose human assumptions in data curation and objectives, even when training data has no labels.

title: Position: Unlabeled $\not =$ No Human Supervision in Visual Learning

abstract: Despite the proliferation of Explainable AI (XAI) techniques—from feature attributions to sparse autoencoders—explanations rarely influence real-world workflows. In practice, they are often generated and discarded without guiding meaningful action. This gap reflects foundational shortcomings: research has not yet established methodologies for integrating explanations into end-to-end, human-in-the-loop systems. This position paper argues that the machine learning community must pivot from ad-hoc XAI methods toward addressing foundational & structural challenges, including unclear problem formulations, underspecified evaluation objectives, and the absence of pipelines for explanation-driven feedback. We support this claim through an analysis of recent ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR papers and a survey of XAI practitioners, revealing recurring issues that limit cumulative progress. We conclude by outlining a practical checklist designed to shift XAI toward a more human-centered, action-oriented paradigm. By emphasizing foundational clarity over the development of ad-hoc methods, we hope to provide a roadmap for integrating explanations into actionable, feedback-driven AI systems.

paragraphs: Explainable AI has produced many techniques for describing model behavior, but the authors argue that those descriptions rarely change real-world workflows. An explanation can be generated successfully and still be discarded without affecting a decision. The paper treats this gap as a problem in how explainability research is formulated and connected to human use.

The authors support their position through an analysis of recent ICML, NeurIPS, and ICLR papers and a survey of explainability practitioners. They identify recurring structural issues: unclear problem definitions, evaluation goals that are insufficiently specified, and missing processes for turning explanation-based feedback into changes. These issues limit the field’s ability to build cumulatively toward useful systems.

The paper proposes a practical checklist for making explainability more human-centered and oriented toward action. Its emphasis is on complete workflows in which people inspect explanations, provide feedback, and influence what happens next. The intended shift makes integration and evaluation central research problems, so that progress reflects how explanations support meaningful decisions rather than simply their production.
summary.tldr: Explainability research should clarify its goals and build feedback workflows that turn explanations into useful human action.

Crafting Papers on Machine Learning
Stock Trading System Using Reinforcement Learning with Cooperative Agents

abstract: Most of the existing approaches to collaborative filtering cannot handle very large data sets. In this paper we show how a class of two-layer undirected graphical models, called Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBM’s), can be used to model tabular data, such as user’s ratings of movies. We present efficient learning and inference procedures for this class of models and demonstrate that RBM’s can be successfully applied to the Netflix data set, containing over 100 million user/movie ratings. We also show that RBM’s slightly outperform carefully-tuned SVD models. When the predictions of multiple RBM models and multiple SVD models are linearly combined, we achieve an error rate that is well over 6% better than the score of Netflix’s own system.

We present efficient learning and inference procedures for this class of models and demonstrate that RBM’s can be successfully applied to the Netflix data set, containing over 100 million user/movie ratings. paragraphs: Collaborative filtering uses patterns in data such as users' movie ratings to make predictions. This paper addresses the difficulty of handling very large rating datasets with existing approaches. It shows how Restricted Boltzmann Machines, a class of two-layer undirected graphical models, can represent tabular data of this kind.

The authors provide efficient procedures for both learning the models and using them for inference. They demonstrate the approach on the Netflix dataset, which contains more than 100 million user–movie ratings. This application establishes that the proposed modeling and computational procedures can operate successfully at the scale of that dataset.

The reported RBM models slightly outperform carefully tuned singular-value-decomposition models. A larger improvement comes from linearly combining predictions from multiple RBMs and multiple SVD models: the combined predictor achieves an error score well over 6% better than Netflix's own system. These are distinct findings. The individual RBMs deliver a modest advantage over the tuned SVD comparison, while the stronger reported improvement belongs to the combined ensemble.
summary.tldr: RBMs scale to the Netflix ratings dataset, slightly beat tuned SVD models, and contribute to a stronger combined predictor.

title: Restricted Boltzmann machines for collaborative filtering

abstract: We study the problem of learning kernel machines transductively for structured output variables. Transductive learning can be reduced to combinatorial optimization problems over all possible labelings of the unlabeled data. In order to scale transductive learning to structured variables, we transform the corresponding non-convex, combinatorial, constrained optimization problems into continuous, unconstrained optimization problems. The discrete optimization parameters are eliminated and the resulting differentiable problems can be optimized efficiently. We study the effectiveness of the generalized TSVM on multiclass classification and labelsequence learning problems empirically.
originalAbstract: We study the problem of learning kernel machines transductively for structured output variables. Transductive learning can be reduced to combinatorial optimization problems over all possible labelings of the unlabeled data. In order to scale transductive learning to structured variables, we transform the corresponding non-convex, combinatorial, constrained optimization problems into continuous, unconstrained optimization problems. The discrete optimization parameters are eliminated and the resulting differentiable problems can be optimized efficiently. We study the effectiveness of the generalized TSVM on multiclass classification and labelsequence learning problems empirically.

paragraphs: Transductive learning incorporates unlabeled examples into the learning problem by considering their possible labels. With structured outputs, such as label sequences, each example can have many candidate assignments. Searching across combinations of those assignments creates a combinatorial optimization problem. This paper studies how to make transductive kernel machines workable in that setting.

The authors transform the original nonconvex, constrained problems, which contain discrete choices, into continuous optimization problems without constraints. The discrete optimization parameters are eliminated, and the resulting objectives are differentiable. This reformulation changes how the search can be performed: it permits efficient continuous optimization instead of directly handling the original discrete label-assignment variables.

The resulting generalized transductive support vector machine is evaluated empirically on multiclass classification and label-sequence learning. These applications examine the approach across both class selection and structured prediction. The abstract identifies efficient optimization as a central benefit of the reformulation; it does not claim that differentiability makes the problem convex or guarantees a globally optimal solution.
summary.tldr: The paper reformulates transductive learning for structured outputs as differentiable, unconstrained optimization and evaluates a generalized transductive SVM.

title: Transductive support vector machines for structured variables

abstract: Approximate linear programming (ALP) is a reinforcement learning technique with nice theoretical properties, but it often performs poorly in practice. We identify some reasons for the poor quality of ALP solutions in problems where the approximation induces virtual loops. We then introduce two methods for improving solution quality. One method rolls out selected constraints of the ALP, guided by the dual information. The second method is a relaxation of the ALP, based on external penalty methods. The latter method is applicable in domains in which rolling out constraints is impractical. Both approaches show promising empirical results for simple benchmark problems as well as for a more realistic blood inventory management problem.

paragraphs: Approximate linear programming is a reinforcement learning technique with attractive theoretical properties, yet its practical solutions can be poor. This paper investigates that gap in problems where the approximation creates virtual loops. Identifying this source of difficulty motivates changes to the optimization constraints that determine the resulting solution.

The authors propose two approaches. The first rolls out selected constraints, using information from the dual optimization problem to guide which constraints receive this treatment. The second relaxes the approximate linear program through external penalty methods. This provides an alternative for domains where rolling out constraints is impractical, so the two methods address different computational circumstances.

Both approaches produce promising empirical results on simple benchmark problems and on a more realistic blood inventory management problem. The findings connect a diagnosis of approximation-related trouble with concrete ways to improve solution quality. Their significance is practical: modifying how constraints are handled can help address weaknesses in approximate linear programming, including settings where the rollout-based remedy cannot readily be applied.
summary.tldr: Two constraint-handling methods address poor approximate linear programming solutions associated with virtual loops and show promising empirical results.

title: Constraint relaxation in approximate linear programs

abstract: We consider principal component analysis for contaminated data-set in the high dimensional regime, where the number of observations is comparable or more than the dimensionality of each observation. We propose a *deterministic* high-dimensional robust PCA algorithm which inherits all theoretical properties of its *randomized* counterpart, i.e., it is tractable, robust to contaminated points, easily kernelizable, asymptotic consistent and achieves maximal robustness - a breakdown point of 50%. More importantly, the proposed method exhibits significantly better computational efficiency, which makes it suitable for large-scale real applications.
originalAbstract: We consider principal component analysis for contaminated data-set in the high dimensional regime, where the number of observations is comparable or more than the dimensionality of each observation. We propose a *deterministic* high-dimensional robust PCA algorithm which inherits all theoretical properties of its *randomized* counterpart, i.e., it is tractable, robust to contaminated points, easily kernelizable, asymptotic consistent and achieves maximal robustness - a breakdown point of 50%. More importantly, the proposed method exhibits significantly better computational efficiency, which makes it suitable for large-scale real applications.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis seeks a compact representation of variation in data, but contaminated observations complicate that task. This paper considers robust PCA in a high-dimensional regime where the number of observations is comparable to or greater than the dimension of each observation. It proposes a deterministic alternative to an existing randomized approach.

The new algorithm retains the theoretical properties of its randomized counterpart. These include tractability, resistance to contaminated points, compatibility with kernelization, and asymptotic consistency. It also retains the stated maximal robustness of a 50% breakdown point. These properties make robustness part of the algorithm's theoretical foundation, rather than only an observed outcome.

The principal improvement is computational efficiency: the deterministic method is reported to be significantly faster while preserving those guarantees. That combination matters for large applications, where a robust procedure must also be practical to run. The paper's contribution is therefore a more efficient way to obtain the established robust-PCA properties, with the authors identifying large-scale real applications as a suitable use.
summary.tldr: A deterministic robust-PCA algorithm improves computational efficiency while retaining its randomized counterpart's guarantees, including a 50% breakdown point.

title: Robust PCA in High-dimension: A Deterministic Approach

abstract: We describe a nonparametric topic model for labeled data. The model uses a mixture of random measures (MRM) as a base distribution of the Dirichlet process (DP) of the HDP framework, so we call it the DP-MRM. To model labeled data, we define a DP distributed random measure for each label, and the resulting model generates an unbounded number of topics for each label. We apply DP-MRM on single-labeled and multi-labeled corpora of documents and compare the performance on label prediction with LDA-SVM and Labeled-LDA. We further enhance the model by incorporating ddCRP and modeling multi-labeled images for image segmentation and object labeling, comparing the performance with nCuts and rddCRP.

The model uses a mixture of random measures (MRM) as a base distribution of the Dirichlet process (DP) of the HDP framework, so we call it the DP-MRM. To model labeled data, we define a DP distributed random measure for each label, and the resulting model generates an unbounded number of topics for each label. We further enhance the model by incorporating ddCRP and modeling multi-labeled images for image segmentation and object labeling, comparing the performance with nCuts and rddCRP.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a topic model for data with labels, including examples that have more than one label. Its central modeling choice is to let each label be associated with an unbounded collection of topics. This gives labels a richer internal structure than a single fixed topic and avoids imposing a finite topic count for each label.

The model, called DP-MRM, modifies the hierarchical Dirichlet process framework by using a mixture of random measures as a base distribution. Each label receives its own Dirichlet-process-distributed random measure. These label-specific components form the basis of a model that connects observed labels with latent topics while retaining a nonparametric topic representation.

The authors apply DP-MRM to document collections with single and multiple labels, comparing label prediction with LDA-SVM and Labeled-LDA. They also incorporate ddCRP for image segmentation and object labeling in images with multiple labels, comparing with nCuts and rddCRP. These applications demonstrate the scope of the proposed framework across text and images; the abstract reports the comparisons without claiming a particular performance advantage.
summary.tldr: DP-MRM models labeled data with an unbounded number of topics per label and is applied to document prediction and image labeling.

title: Dirichlet Process with Mixed Random Measures: A Nonparametric Topic Model for Labeled Data
